articles.body:
Six weeks of campaigning, politicking and debates is done. New Zealand has voted and over the next few hours we’ll find out the results of what has been cast as one of the tightest elections in recent memory.

For weeks, the polls have shown no clear path to government for any potential coalition, left or right. Seemingly unimpressed by National and Labour, polls have tracked voters turning to the smaller parties, such as the centrist Opportunity party.

Tonight could see Opportunity potentially end up as kingmaker, unless that pre-election support and hype has failed to translate into votes. Stay with us as we learn the answer to that big question and others, as we keep you across the counts and results as they come in. It’s going to be an exciting night!

For anyone tuning in who needs a refresher on the MMP electoral system, here goes:

MMP means voters are asked to vote twice – once for their preferred party and the second time for an electorate MP.

There is a single chamber of parliament which generally has 120 MPs. This is the overhang issue which I think we’re going to be talking about tonight as results come in.

Under MMP it is very uncommon for a single party to form a government.

If there is no majority winner, the major parties will start negotiations after the election and can either form a coalition or confidence-and-supply agreements with minor parties. The party with the largest number of votes does not necessarily win, and negotiations can take days or weeks.

Some senior National heavy hitters will, remarkably, be out of a job if National’s party vote goes badly tonight.

Those most at risk include:

Nicola Willis (finance minister), Chris Bishop (like Willis, is tipped as a potential future leader of the party), Paul Goldsmith (justice minister) and Gerry Brownlee (speaker of the house).

Some background: All the pre-election polls looked bad for any National MP who was relying on the list vote to return them to parliament; such as Willis and Brownlee, who are list-only candidates. Goldsmith (Epsom) and Bishop (Hutt South) are both engaged in tense, marginal electorate battles. If either loses, they are then reliant on winning via the list. We’ll be watching all this closely.

Some of the Labour party candidates are locked in neck and neck races, with tensions high for those at the Labour party event watching the candidates in Hutt South. With more than 20% of the vote counted, Labour’s Ginny Anderson has edged just ahead of the incumbent, National MP Chris Bishop, by just a handful of ballots.

Green MP Julie-Anne Genter is just holding off Labour challenger Craig Renney in Wellington North, while Labour’s Kieran McAnulty is winning against National’s Mike Butterick in Wairarapa.

Elsewhere in Wellington, Labour party MP Ayesha Verrall was hoping to win Wellington North off the incumbent Green MP Tamatha Paul, but early votes suggest this won’t be the case. Paul is leading comfortably, at almost twice Verrall’s count in an electorate where Green is also leading the party vote.

Another key feature of this election has been the possibility of an overhang - where a party wins more electorates than its share of the party vote.

If that occurs, more seats will be added to parliament to make up the difference and could dictate which coalition can form a government.

Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) has been calling on supporters to engineer an overhang for its party - by voting for its candidates in the Māori seats, and not giving them a party vote. This could benefit the left bloc.

Meanwhile, if National holds on to a good portion of its seats but its party vote falls short, that will give the party an edge to form a government but could see some of its most prominent MPs out of parliament.

Elsewhere in the Upper Hutt Cosmopolitan Club, punters were ordering crate bottles of local beer Tui and listening to a band kick up a rendition of Tennessee Whiskey.

For Hutt locals, the Cossie Club is a social hub; karaoke on Thursdays, Bingo on Sundays, and a jug of lager for $14 during happy hour.

While everyone spoken to by The Guardian voted for Hipkins in the Remutaka electorate – “he’s a local boy,” – party votes were otherwise split between Labour, the Opportunity party, and NZ First.

“I’ve always voted Labour, Chris knows that,” said Gladys Cooney, 96. “I haven’t heard anything from them this election, I don’t think anyone has gone deep enough.” The cost of living was appalling, she said. “Everything you touch has gone up.”

Fellow local Paul O’Riley also voted for Hipkins, but party voted NZ First. “I worked for 50 years in this country as a truck driver, Winston [Peters] does the most for us.”

Seven of the seats in New Zealand’s 120-seat parliamentare Māori electorates. Voters of Māori descent can choose to vote on the Māori roll – allowing them to vote for these seats – or the general roll. More than half of Māori voters are on the Māori roll.

They still get two votes; one for the electorate, and one for their preferred political party.

Last election, Te Pāti Māori won six of the seven seats. But internal turmoil has plagued the party since. Tonight, eyes will be on Te Tai Tokerau – covering the geographical area from New Zealand’s most northern point in Cape Reinga to West Auckland – where the Green’s candidate Hūhana Lyndon could help the party nab their first Māori seat.

Latest polls put her leading the race, followed by Labour’s Willow-Jean Prime and Te Pāti Māori candidate Aperahama Edwards.

Te Pāti Māori remain ahead in most other electorates, aside from Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and Te Tai Tonga (the biggest electorate, covering the entirety of the South Island and Stewart Island) where Labour candidates lead polling.

In an election night that has come down to Chris vs Chris, it’s important to know the difference.

Christopher Luxon, 56, the incumbent, leader of the National party and PM since 2023, is the former chief executive of the country’s national airline, Air New Zealand, and previously worked a slew of corporate jobs worldwide. He entered parliament in 2020, winning the Auckland electorate of Botany. A father-of-two, he is Christian but doesn’t discuss his faith, and has emphasised his business credentials — in 2023, his party was elected on its economic pledges.

Chris Hipkins, 48, the career politician who leads the center-left Labour party, is having a second crack at being PM tonight. Following the resignation of Jacinda Ardern in January 2023, Hipkins, also a father of two, took the reins for nine months ahead of that election, which his party lost. He’s held the Remutaka electorate in parliament since 2008. Some voters still associate him with Covid-19 and strict lockdown measures, while others connect with his pledges for better healthcare and improved cost of living.

National party faithful are starting to trickle into its event at the cavernous Viaduct Event Centre on Auckland’s waterfront. The room is awash in blue light.

People are grabbing drinks and milling around. The reaction is flicking between nervousness and excitement as the first numbers show the race is - as predicted - neck and neck.

As the first results of the night flashed up onto the big screen, Labour party volunteer Jasmine, 22, who works in the public service and didn’t want to use her last name, stopped talking mid-sentence.

A hush fell over the room as the first poll results show the main parties neck and neck . “That’s close,” she said, exhaling. “It’s great that Opportunity is over 5%, I’m happy about that. It’s just overwhelming; this is years of work, and that’s real numbers.” She’s been working for the party since she was 16.

Cheers are going up in the room as electorate results begin to come in. About 200 party supporters are expected here tonight.

articles.body:
The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans.

But as Israel took stock of the results, there was also a sense that the elections marked a longer-term shift in US politics that will make the job of any new Israeli leader far more difficult.

The United States provides Israel with critical military and diplomatic support, so nurturing bipartisan ties was the cornerstone of foreign policy for decades. Netanyahu ripped up that commitment to throw his lot in with the Republicans in general and Trump in particular.

The opposition had always attacked his decision as ill-judged. By the end of the week, they were warning that it was positively dangerous.

“These people aren’t against Israel,” prominent opposition politician Yair Lapid said of incoming Democratic lawmakers, urging his country to rebuild bridges. “They’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.”

“The easiest thing is to scream that ‘America is lost,’ because if it’s lost, you don’t have to work. That’s just not true. Not at all.”

Lapid laid out a plan to “rebuild trust” in the US, but it perhaps did more to demonstrate the scale of the problem than reassure Israelis.

His proposal of a transatlantic charm offensive by officials of a prospective new government drew a swift and sharp rebuke from the New York congressman-elect Brad Lander.

Lander, a Democrat who is Jewish and describes himself as a liberal Zionist, was detained in the occupied West Bank last month while joining Palestinians trying to harvest olives.

“Minister Lapid: As someone who won a seat in Congress last night, and who cares about Israel: you’re not listening to what American voters – Jewish and non-Jewish – are saying,” Lander wrote in a direct response.

“We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”

In his exchange with Lapid, Lander also highlighted the arrest of journalist Abed Abu Shehada, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, as an example of how Israel violates international law. He drew a direct link with the ICE “regime of detention without charges, based on secret evidence, designed to intimidate and chill speech” that he said was rejected by US voters.

Abu Shehada was reportedly taken from his home by 15 masked security officials in a night-time raid, without an arrest warrant. Interrogators have only questioned him about a podcast interview with a public figure, lawyers acting for Abu Shehada said.

On Friday, Lander and two other incoming Jewish members of Congress, Daniel Bliss and Scott Wiener, wrote to Israel’s ambassador to the US calling for the immediate release of Abu Shehada.

“Detaining a reporter for conducting an interview — the only issue that interrogators questioned him about — is a violation of international law,” Lander said when he published the letter. “It comes at a time when senior Israeli officials are trying to delegitimize the participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s recent elections.”

Nor do Israel’s problems end with angry Democrats. The wounded Republican establishment lost no time looking a few thousand miles away to find reasons for the collapse of its voter base.

Soon after the election results came in, the vice-president, JD Vance, put “our relationship with Israel” on a short list of reasons for voter fury, and on election day Trump made a last-ditch attempt to woo voters with a pledge to cut off $4bn (£3bn) in annual military aid to Israel.

The announcement caused panic in Israel’s defence establishment. “When the commander of the Israel air force hears something like that, he might slit his wrists,” one official told Channel 12 news. “Where are we going to come up with 15 billion shekels every year, and what does that mean for Israel’s future defence budget?”

Netanyahu only responded to Trump’s electioneering on Friday with an attempt to spin the cut as a joint decision reflecting Israel’s economic strength. It demonstrated a “move from aid to partnership”, his office said in a statement.

Netanyahu has long flaunted his relationship with Trump, his fluent English and experience in the US, presenting himself as the only man with the international standing to guarantee Israel’s security in a hostile world.

After Tuesday’s US election, he looks more like an agent of its destruction to many in Israel. “One thing is clear: we are losing America,” Ben Caspit wrote in Ma’ariv, a daily newspaper.

“This isn’t a process; it isn’t happening in stages; it is happening all at once. It is an avalanche. It is a reverberating collapse of the foundation of Israel’s national defence doctrine. This isn’t a decree of fate. It is a decree of Netanyahu.”

Some advocates for change inside Israel found cause for hope in the Democrats’ victory, if Israel’s opposition can turn their mandate for change into a new government. They won 67 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but more than a quarter went to Palestinian citizens of Israel, and some of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out sitting with them.

US administrations have for too long equated support for Israel with blind support for its government, said Nadav Tamir, a former senior Israeli diplomat in the US who is now executive director of J Street Israel.

That consensus is cracking, but the majority of lawmakers from both parties still see Israel as a key US ally in the Middle East, he wrote in the Times of Israel.

External pressure from those who support its security but see current policy as self-destructive might push the country towards necessary change, including a resolution of the Israel-Palestine conflict.

“Perhaps this will be the paradox of the new [US] Congress,” he wrote. “It will be less willing to define support for Israel as automatic alignment with every policy of its government, but precisely for that reason, it may offer Israel more meaningful support in breaking out of the cycle of wars and building a future of security and prosperity.”

articles.title: President Herzog faces key choice as Israel struggles to form government
articles.summary: Eisenkot's bloc and Arab-led parties seek to oust Netanyahu, but failure to form government could leave him in power.
articles.preview: Palestinian-led parties have backed Eisenkot in a bid to oust Netanyahu, but the prime minister could stay on if no government is formed. Israeli President Isaac Herzog must decide who gets the first attempt at forming a government, after an inconclusive election left both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, short of a parliamentary majority. Herzog has said he will task a candidate with forming a government on Sunday.
articles.body:
Palestinian-led parties have backed Eisenkot in a bid to oust Netanyahu, but the prime minister could stay on if no government is formed.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog must decide who gets the first attempt at forming a government, after an inconclusive election left both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, short of a parliamentary majority.

Herzog has said he will task a candidate with forming a government on Sunday. Eisenkot has received the endorsement of a majority of lawmakers – but only thanks to parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record 19 seats in October’s election, but whom Eisenkot has ruled out bringing into government.

Here is what we know:

Who is Herzog likely to ask to form a government?

During consultations between party heads and Herzog, which ended on Thursday, 67 out of 120 Knesset members endorsed Eisenkot, while only 46 endorsed Netanyahu.

Netanyahu’s endorsements fell seven short of his bloc’s 53 seats after United Torah Judaism, one of his longtime allies, withheld endorsements over his coalition’s failure to exempt ultra-Orthodox Israelis from military service.

Herzog has not publicly committed to either side, saying that while the numbers may look clear, “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” made it hard to tell who could build a coalition.

Prior to the October 27 elections, reports emerged that the president wanted to push for a national unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s rival parties to avoid another election.

How difficult will it be to form a government?

No bloc has secured the 61 seats needed to form a majority government. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious alliance has 53, four Jewish-led parties backing Eisenkot hold 48, and the Arab-led parties hold 19.

Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.

United Torah Judaism has signalled that its support was available for the right price, but Shas endorsed Netanyahu on Wednesday.

Netanyahu, meanwhile, would need to lure an opposition party to his side. A unity government with the two men rotating as prime minister – and excluding Arab-led parties from government – is another option, but many Netanyahu rivals have ruled out serving under him.

Will Arab-led parties be part of the next government?

So far, it seems unlikely that they will.

The Arab-led parties are the Joint List, an alliance of three parties, and the United Arab List (Ra’am). They hold 11 and eight seats, respectively.

Ra’am says it is willing to join an Eisenkot-led government, while the Joint List has ruled out joining but offered to help put him in office from the outside.

Both endorsed Eisenkot during consultations with President Herzog, but he has refused to bring either into government unless they meet certain conditions, including recognising Hamas as a “terrorist organisation”.

Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas, whose party joined an anti-Netanyahu coalition in 2021 and became the first party representing Palestinians to enter government in Israel, has expressed support for disarming Hamas, but declined to label it as a “terror” group.

However, Israeli law allows Eisenkot to become prime minister with fewer than 61 seats if his proposed government wins a parliamentary confidence vote – which the two could help him secure.

Eisenkot could form a minority government in the meantime and later secure a majority by luring the two ultra-Orthodox parties by making concessions on the conscription issue.

In positions that many observers see as highlighting the second-class nature of Palestinian citizens in Israel, some of Eisenkot’s allies have opposed any reliance on Palestinian lawmakers, while Netanyahu’s Likud has threatened that cooperating with the Arab-led parties would be “dangerous to Israel”.

Senior Joint List member Ahmad Tibi told The Associated Press that rejecting a partnership would prove Israel is “an ethnocracy, not an absolute democracy for all citizens”.

What do Palestinian-led parties want from the next government?

First, an end to Netanyahu’s rule.

The Joint List said its unanimous backing for Eisenkot answered a “public demand” to stop Netanyahu and his government returning to power.

By widening Eisenkot’s lead, it said, it hoped to narrow the path to a unity government that keeps Netanyahu in office. Its support, it added, did not mean dropping its reservations about an opposition that had not shown readiness to confront Netanyahu’s approach or incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel.

In return for outside support, Arab-led parties are seeking guarantees for Palestinian citizens, including an end to house demolitions and incitement, action against crime, and a political horizon for Palestinians.

Tibi told The AP he had no illusions that this would end Israel’s wars or bring a Palestinian state, but said a “repair government” would improve Palestinian citizens’ lives, including, potentially, by tackling violent crime in their communities.

Ra’am leader Abbas has also said ending the government of Netanyahu, and far-right figures such as Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, is a priority.

What happens if no government can be formed?

The nominee chosen by Herzog will have 28 days to form a coalition, extendable by 14 more. If they fail, another nominee will be chosen and granted 28 days.

If the second nominee fails, a parliament majority can back a third candidate, and be granted a final 14 days.

If once again no government is formed, the Knesset will be dissolved and an entirely new election called within 90 days. This would mean Netanyahu staying on as caretaker prime minister.

Nehru Jamhour, an analyst of Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera that this drawn-out impasse was the likeliest outcome, and Netanyahu’s preferred one. He said that Netanyahu was hoping that a repeat election could weaken his rivals and depress turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

articles.title: In Sudafrica l’Anc non fa più presa nelle città
articles.summary: I sudafricani hanno votato per le amministrative con in mente i problemi causati dalla cattiva gestione dei servizi pubblici. Per l’African national congress il verdetto è stato duro
articles.preview: Il 4 novembre, mentre il resto del mondo era concentrato sui risultati delle elezioni di metà mandato negli Stati Uniti, i sudafricani sono andati alle urne per rinnovare più di 10.500 consigli municipali, tra cui quelli delle otto città metropolitane, che comprendono centri importanti come Pretoria, Johannesburg, Città del Capo, Durban e Bloemfontein. La legge sudafricana non prevede l’elezione diretta del sindaco, che viene scelto dal nuovo consiglio locale entro 14 giorni dal voto.
articles.body:
Il 4 novembre, mentre il resto del mondo era concentrato sui risultati delle elezioni di metà mandato negli Stati Uniti, i sudafricani sono andati alle urne per rinnovare più di 10.500 consigli municipali, tra cui quelli delle otto città metropolitane, che comprendono centri importanti come Pretoria, Johannesburg, Città del Capo, Durban e Bloemfontein.

La legge sudafricana non prevede l’elezione diretta del sindaco, che viene scelto dal nuovo consiglio locale entro 14 giorni dal voto. Quindi le preferenze di elettori ed elettrici – la cui affluenza alle urne è stata del al 54,5 per cento, in crescita rispetto al 2021 – non si rivolgono a singoli candidati, ma hanno anche un importante valore di termometro politico, in particolare sull’operato dell’African national congress (Anc), il partito nato dal movimento di liberazione guidato da Nelson Mandela, che è al potere dalla fine dell’apartheid, nel 1994.

Come previsto prima del voto, il verdetto è stato spietato. Già dai risultati parziali delle elezioni amministrative è apparso chiaramente che il partito del presidente Cyril Ramaphosa ha perso gran parte di quel consenso e di quella legittimità che gli avevano permesso di governare indisturbato per trent’anni. E li ha persi a causa dei pessimi servizi pubblici erogati alla popolazione, a cominciare dalla distribuzione dell’acqua potabile.

Un’immagine del vignettista Zapiro riassume bene la situazione: dalla torre per le telecomunicazioni, simbolo di Johannesburg, sporge un rubinetto – gestito dall’Anc – da cui esce un’unica goccia d’acqua, che cade nel secchio vuoto dei voti per il partito. Sullo sfondo, alcune persone fanno la fila per prendere l’acqua da un camion cisterna. “È a secco!”, commenta un funzionario vestito con i colori del partito. “Chissà come mai…”, risponde una signora.

Uno dei temi principali della campagna elettorale è stato proprio l’accesso all’acqua potabile, uno dei problemi più gravi per le popolazioni urbane del Sudafrica, in un contesto generale di dissesto finanziario, infrastrutture carenti o in stato di abbandono, interruzioni di corrente elettrica e cattiva gestione della raccolta dei rifiuti.

Secondo il sito sudafricano Groundup, in più della metà delle città che si occupano del trattamento dell’acqua la qualità di quest’ultima è insoddisfacente, se non pessima. E, anche se la qualità dell’acqua è buona, le amministrazioni locali non sono sempre in grado di distribuirla efficacemente, a causa delle perdite nella rete idrica. Il risultato è che in alcune aree i residenti restano senz’acqua corrente per giorni. Secondo Groundup la situazione di oggi è leggermente migliore rispetto ai tempi della presidenza di Jacob Zuma (2009-2018), nota come il “decennio perduto” a causa dei livelli altissimi di corruzione e di appropriazione indebita delle risorse pubbliche. Ma c’è ancora molto lavoro da fare.

L’Anc ne ha pagato il conto. Il declino non è recente, come mostra questa mappa: se nel 2004 aveva ottenuto quasi il 70 per cento dei voti a livello nazionale, alle amministrative del 2021 il partito era sceso per la prima volta sotto il 50 per cento. Alle politiche del 2024 aveva registrato poco più del 40 per cento dei voti a suo favore ed era stato costretto per la prima volta a formare un governo di unità nazionale con altri nove partiti, tra cui la Democratic alliance (Da), il partito di riferimento della minoranza bianca. Dal suo feudo di Città del Capo, la Da, guidata da Helen Zille, 75 anni, ha cominciato a fare presa anche nel resto del paese, tanto che oggi rischia di strappare all’Anc il controllo di Pretoria e di Johannesburg, il motore economico del paese.

Zille, che in passato è stata criticata per le sue posizioni sulla questione razziale, si è proposta come candidata sindaca di Joburg, scommettendo sul fatto che i cittadini siano più interessati a temi come la qualità della vita e dei servizi, che alla sua appartenenza razziale. E il voto potrebbe non darle torto. Con queste elezioni l’Anc è diventato un “partito di campagna”, scrive il commentatore del Financial Times David Pilling.

La formazione è ancora radicata nelle zone rurali, ma è in caduta libera nelle grandi città, dove si fanno sentire di più i disservizi e gli altri problemi che affliggono il paese, come l’insicurezza dovuta alla criminalità e alla violenza politica (solo all’avvicinarsi di queste elezioni sono stati registrati venti casi di omicidi a sfondo politico). Se a livello nazionale i risultati preliminari danno l’Anc al 32 per cento, con la Da al 24 per cento, in città come Johannesburg e Pretoria il partito di Zille è decisamente in testa. A Durban, il più grande porto del paese, invece è andato forte il partito uMkhonto we Sizwe (Mk), dell’ex presidente Zuma, la Da è seconda e l’Anc terzo.

Si aprirà presto una fase di intense trattative per formare coalizioni stabili in grado di governare le grandi città del paese. L’Anc e la Da sono già partner nel governo nazionale dal 2024, e finora la loro alleanza ha resistito nonostante le molte divergenze. “Molti elettori sudafricani stanno cominciando a non votare più in base a criteri razziali ed etnici… per scegliere in base alla competenza” dei candidati, nota il commentatore sudafricano William Gumede sul Mail & Guardian. La speranza è che i vincitori di queste elezioni amministrative si dimostrino all’altezza.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Africana.

articles.title: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?
articles.summary: Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. articles.preview: Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.
articles.body:
It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”

“They have decided that there is no appetite for negotiation, with the US out of Paris,” said another developing country diplomat. “Countries won’t engage.”

The summit ended with a deal, although few loved it. But, as the faultlines from the Brazilian decision deepen going into this year’s summit, it is clear that the Paris agreement, and climate action around the world, has reached an impasse.

And it is not just Cop insiders who are worried. For many outside the vast white air-conditioned conference halls, the question, as this year’s summit begins, will be: what is the point?

Those same governments have pledged year after year since the Paris agreement was signed in 2015 – and entered into force a year later – to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Yet temperatures for two years have exceeded that threshold, and the UN revealed a few weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate was now for about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating.

There could be no clearer evidence that the Paris agreement, on the face of it, has failed. It is impossible not to wonder whether the Cop process itself is just not fit for purpose.

The charge sheet against Paris is long, with the central issue being the failure to achieve its goal. Beyond that immediate failure, the negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris “rulebook” under which the treaty is interpreted and put into effect.

The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein. Donald Trump’s allies – in Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and some other petrostates – frequently veto measures and obstruct progress.

It took more than 30 years of negotiation since the UN framework convention on climate change was signed in 1992 for fossil fuels even to be addressed directly. This was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away from fossil fuels” but failed to set a timeframe or any policies to back up the resolution.

The US, the world’s biggest economy and responsible for about one in every eight tonnes of carbon dioxide emitted today, has withdrawn from Paris under President Trump.

Even parts of the developed world which support the process have mostly failed to come up with convincing plans: Australia, co-host of Cop31, has set no end to fossil fuel exports; its fellow co-host Turkey plans to increase its carbon output. The UK is opening a gasfield and mulling a new oilfield, Germany has dropped its electric vehicle sales targets and scrapped a renewable heating law. Meanwhile, most rich countries are reducing their contributions to climate finance for the poor.

Most of all, the slow pace of the Paris timetable might have seemed fine in 2015, when temperatures were rising at 0.2C a decade. Today, the rate of rise is 0.4C a decade and still accelerating.

“The structures of Cops and Paris are labyrinthine, bureaucratic, and ultimately dispiriting,” said Paul Bledsoe, a former Clinton White House climate adviser, now with the American University. “It may be time to streamline them to focus more deliberately on national emissions reduction goals.”

As ordinary people watch these failures outside and inside the process, some are losing faith. The Paris agreement was a sensation, celebrated around the world. In the years since, the aura of Cop has faded, as meetings seem to disintegrate into arguments over wording and compromise.

“A lot of the commitments, the promises that were made, just turned out to be a bunch of hot air,” said Juan Carlos Monterrey, former climate envoy for Panama, now chief executive of the Vanglabs consultancy. “Under that measure, we have failed.”

Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said: “The fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast, that Earth’s resilience is showing worrying signs of decline, and that we still allow ourselves to follow a global path that will take us to a catastrophic 2.6C-3C, and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”

But, like most involved in international climate efforts, both refuse to concede that Paris is done for. “On the other hand,” said Rockström, “Paris is all we have. And we know that the global climate crisis can only, in the end, be solved if all countries in the world simultaneously move away from planet-damaging heat injection.”

Monterrey agrees. The most important fact about the Paris agreement, and the Cop process, he says, is that they exist. “Paris is our moral compass. It has told us where we should go. The speed of travel is not what it needs to be, but Paris has set the direction.”

A messy compromise

This year’s Cop is the first to have a split presidency and host. Being held in Turkey but presided over by Australia, Cop31 is a messy compromise between two countries whose other chief point of commonality is an admiration for coal.

Unexpectedly, however, the skies are a little brighter over this year’s meeting than anyone might have expected. Brazil has decisively re-elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva who has already overseen the biggest reductions in deforestation for decades.

The US midterms delivered a drubbing for the right, while in Serbia and Hungary this year democracy has won out over authoritarianism. Though the far right is still on the march across much of Europe, and autocrats still rule in most of the countries with the biggest fossil fuel industries and highest emissions, the replacement or weakening of anti-climate authoritarians by pro-climate parties is a positive sign. Globally, a large majority of people support climate action.

Action beyond the framework of Cop is marching on. After the failure of last year’s Cop30 in Brazil to provide a strong statement on phasing out fossil fuels, a group of nearly 60 countries held an alternative meeting in Colombia in April and agreed to draw up their own national roadmaps for the “transition away from fossil fuels”.

Three major countries have so far done so: France, Germany and the Netherlands. Bledsoe wants to use this model for more side agreements on the “super pollutants” such as methane, refrigerant chemicals called HFCs, ground-level ozone, nitrous oxide and black carbon, or soot.

Cutting methane by 40% could alone hold down temperatures by about 0.3C in the next decade, and deeper cuts beyond that could yield a 0.5C decrease by 2100.

“Paris was never intended to do all the hard work itself,” Bledsoe said. “We need to use the G7, the G20 and other forums too, and we need to elevate the climate to the level of national security concern, and see it as an economic threat.”

While the failures of Paris might seem obvious, its “moral compass” has also translated into greater success in the real world than many people realise.

“The solar panels on my roof and the BYD Dolphin [electric car] my neighbour drives are exhibit one and exhibit two of Paris’s success,” said Claudio Angelo, of the Observatório do Clima thinktank. “Will Paris prevent overshoot of 1.5C? No way. Will it prevent 2C of warming? Unlikely. But the transformation it has triggered can’t be exaggerated.”

Perhaps the clinching argument lies in China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and second-largest economy.

“China is taking multilateral climate efforts more seriously than many other countries, and certainly more seriously than it did a few years ago,” said Li Shuo, director of the China climate hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “The reason is simple: its economic stakes have grown enormously. If the world abandons decarbonisation, where will China sell its solar panels and electric vehicles?”

And, stung by high fossil fuel prices, many developing-country consumers are grasping clean technology without waiting for assistance. In Pakistan, plagued by blackouts and grid supply issues, rooftop solar panels have taken off, now making up about a quarter of electricity use in the country. Similarly, drivers in Vietnam are increasingly opting for cheap electric vehicles from China, which now make up more than 40% of its car sales.

Meanwhile, the conference hosts themselves, from unpromising beginnings, have brought forward one of the biggest new ideas in the last decade for putting the world on track to lower emissions – changing fuel sources for cars and heating to electricity. The electricity should be from clean sources where possible – but its efficiency means that even if the energy source is fossil-based, it still uses less power.

Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University, estimates that the superior efficiency of electricity over fossil fuels will mean that the world’s total final energy use can be halved by switching to electric for everything – meaning we need to generate a lot less, too.

If countries can agree a target at Cop31 of deriving 35% of final energy use from electricity by 2035, up from 23% today, that would be a major boost to decarbonisation efforts. Adair Turner, former chair of the UK’s climate change committee and now co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission thinktank, said: “Electrification is the single most important thing you have to do [to reach net zero emissions].”

Cops provide a place where countries can come together to share experiences, to seek advice, to find support and fellowship. “That’s very valuable,” said Ilana Seid, ambassador of Palau and chair of the Pacific Small Island Developing States. And in a world in which the bulk of current and future emissions, and fossil fuel production, comes from non-democracies or authoritarian states, Cops also provides one of the few forums where they can be held to account.

That “societal pressure” is crucial, said Seid. “We small islands and vulnerable nations are on the frontline. For us, this is existential. We are all very committed to Paris.”

After all, despite all the doubts, the power of a decision at Cop should not be underestimated. While “coalitions of the willing” are a “good thing” according to Nick Stern, the economist, the universality of the Paris agreement and Cops give them a unique authority.

Sue Biniaz, a former US climate negotiator, said: “Any time you have a consensus decision, it sends a signal to investors, to people who finance things, and to countries. I think that’s true these days with the geopolitics of the world – if something can be agreed by the whole world, it’s impactful.”

Cop31 may bring progress on electrification, on climate finance and on the transition that countries, rich and poor, need to make to a low-carbon world. But we already know that whatever the summit produces, it will not be enough.

However flawed yet substantive they are, Cops last only a fortnight, while efforts to tackle the climate crisis will require such wholesale transformation of our economies and societies that they should top governments’ agendas all year.

“Imagine you have lost your loved one without having their bodies to bring back home. Lost livelihood where you spent your whole life to accumulate those assets. We faced a horrific situation,” said Sujeeta Mathema, executive director of ActionAid Nepal, who was quickly on the scene to help people after the catastrophic glacier collapse there.

“It feels like living with grief, fear and uncertainty about the future. The devastation is not just physical; it is deeply emotional and psychological.”

People are traumatised, she says, and deeply feel the injustice of how the climate crisis is created by the rich while hurting the most vulnerable. But Cop can still be a place of hope, Mathema adds.

“Cop is an important space for us to raise our voice, clearly putting our agenda. Cop can help prevent such disasters if the commitments come off paper and are put into action.”

articles.title: US Treasury sanctions eight Canadian money exchange firms over Iran ties
articles.summary: US Treasury claims firms helped sanctioned Iranian entities and handled funds linked to alleged drug trafficking boss.
articles.preview: US Treasury claims firms helped sanctioned Iranian entities and handled funds linked to alleged drug trafficking boss. The United States has imposed sanctions on eight Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping Iranian entities circumvent financial sanctions. The US Department of the Treasury announced the measures on Friday as part of what it calls “Operation Economic Outcast“.
articles.body:
US Treasury claims firms helped sanctioned Iranian entities and handled funds linked to alleged drug trafficking boss.

The United States has imposed sanctions on eight Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping Iranian entities circumvent financial sanctions.

The US Department of the Treasury announced the measures on Friday as part of what it calls “Operation Economic Outcast“.

The Treasury said some of the businesses also laundered their proceeds by converting Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets such as cryptocurrency, adding that some of the businesses helped an alleged head of a drug trafficking ring.

“Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

According to the Treasury, the businesses are based in Ontario and British Columbia, and they include Million Exchange, Amin Exchange and Cryptoyal.

The sanctions effectively cut the firms off from the US dollar-based financial system, freezing any assets they hold in the US and barring them from transactions with American people or entities.

Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) issued a statement shortly after the US Treasury’s announcement, saying that it worked with the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) to impose the sanctions against the money service businesses.

“FINTRAC works regularly with foreign financial intelligence units to combat money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion,” the statement said on Friday. “Through bilateral agreements, the Centre is able to disclose intelligence to financial intelligence units worldwide.”

In a separate statement on Friday, the US Treasury said FinCEN, its anti-money laundering unit, issued an order targeting the money exchanger MEXC Global.

FinCEN said the order prevents US financial institutions from processing fund transfers involving Seychelles-incorporated MEXC Global, which it says has facilitated at least $16bn in illicit transactions linked to Iran, North Korea and Russia, as well as transactions with other sanctioned actors.

More pressure on Tehran

According to the US Treasury, its sanctions campaign aims to “sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime” and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which Canada also lists as a terrorist organisation.

On Wednesday, the US Treasury sanctioned a network in India and Turkiye that it accuses of helping Iran evade restrictions on its oil exports and airlines. The network is run by Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, who are based in the northern Indian city of Chandigarh, the US Treasury said.

The US claimed last week that the campaign had pushed Iran’s rial to new lows and driven inflation to about 90 percent.

Below is a list of the identified businesses in Canada:

- Diverse Trade Inc, doing business as Million Exchange in Ontario

- 1380079 BC Limited, doing business as Amin Exchange in British Columbia

- Top PC Technician Inc, operating in Ontario

- NIA Nations Currency Ltd, based in British Columbia

- 2397639 Ontario Ltd, doing business as Farah Exchange

- CCC Inc in Ontario

- B Galaxy Inc, doing business as Cryptoyal, from the same Ontario location as CCC Inc

- Darvish Exchange in Ontario

articles.title: Cina, dalla bolla immobiliare alla bolla delle auto

articles.body:
A settembre le case automobilistiche cinesi hanno registrato una diminuzione dei profitti pari al 68 per cento rispetto allo stesso periodo di un anno fa. Il calo riguarda quasi tutti i maggiori produttori: nel terzo trimestre del 2026 la Saic Motor, la leader di mercato, ha registrato utili in discesa del 76,7 per cento; la Chongqing Changan Automobile ha perso 760 milioni di yuan (poco più di cento milioni di euro); la Anhui Jianghuai Automobile Group ha avuto una perdita netta di 1,1 miliardi di yuan nei primi nove mesi del 2026; la Seres Group ha registrato un utile netto di 1,4 miliardi di yuan nel terzo trimestre di quest’anno, ma se si escludono le voci non legate alla normale attività dell’azienda risulta una perdita di 1,4 miliardi di yuan. I rappresentanti del settore automobilistico cinese hanno dichiarato che il 2026 potrebbe chiudersi con 18,5 milioni di veicoli venduti, il dato peggiore dal 2014.

Le cause sono l’aumento dei costi e il crollo della domanda interna. Un fatto poco sorprendente in un paese dove la popolazione invecchia costantemente e in generale consuma poco (i consumi cinesi corrispondono al 40 per cento del pil, contro il 70 per cento degli Stati Uniti), i trasporti pubblici sono abbastanza efficienti e i taxi a guida autonoma sono ormai una realtà in molti centri urbani. Per questo sul più grande mercato automobilistico del mondo, spiega il sito Caixin Global, è in corso da tempo una brutale corsa al ribasso dei prezzi tra le numerosissime aziende del settore, una selezione darwiniana che sta mettendo in ginocchio molte di loro.

La posta in gioco

Il dato suscita non pochi interrogativi: com’è possibile che il settore sia in calo mentre il resto del mondo – l’Europa innanzitutto, basta pensare ai guai della Volkswagen – è letteralmente inondato dai veicoli cinesi? La risposta più immediata è che in Cina si è creata una bolla simile a quella che negli scorsi anni ha devastato il settore immobiliare: c’è un forte eccesso di produzione che finora è stato ampiamente assorbito attraverso le esportazioni; ma tutto questo potrebbe non bastare più. Com’è successo nel caso dell’immobiliare, inoltre, non sarà facile assorbire quest’altra bolla, soprattutto perché anche in questo caso, oltre ad aziende e posti di lavoro, è in gioco la stabilità di molti enti locali cinesi, profondamente coinvolti nello sviluppo del settore automobilistico.

Un interessante articolo del Wall Street Journal racconta il caso della Skyworth Auto, un’azienda che nel 2021 sosteneva di poter produrre centomila auto elettriche all’anno, ma che nei primi nove mesi del 2026 ha venduto appena 660 vetture. La Skyworth oggi resta in vita grazie agli aiuti del distretto di Nanchino, che possiede il 5 per cento del suo capitale. Un anno fa, scrive il quotidiano statunitense, sul sito web dell’amministrazione di Nanchino si leggeva che la Skyworth aveva ricevuto “il sostegno completo di tutti i dipartimenti governativi” e che l’aiuto dell’amministrazione aveva permesso di superare “gli ostacoli incontrati dall’azienda nel suo sviluppo”.

La Skyworth non è un’eccezione. Per anni gli enti locali cinesi hanno stretto alleanze con i privati per investire nel settore automobilistico: ogni città puntava sul “campione locale” sperando di diventare la Detroit cinese. Il fenomeno si è accentuato con l’arrivo dell’auto elettrica: alla fine del 2025 le aziende cinesi di auto elettriche che vendevano almeno un modello erano 143. La Nio, azienda pioniere del settore oggi quotata alla borsa di Wall street, stava per dichiarare insolvenza prima che nel 2020 l’amministrazione comunale di Hefei la salvasse con un investimento di quasi settecento milioni di dollari. La città voleva costruire intorno alla Nio un parco industriale dedicato alle auto elettriche con l’obiettivo di dare lavoro a migliaia di persone.

La proliferazione di accordi simili, unita al credito facile concesso dalle banche, ha fatto nascere un settore abnorme in grado di fabbricare 63 milioni di auto all’anno, più del triplo di quelle che nel 2026 dovrebbero essere comprate dai cinesi. Il resto finisce all’estero, su un mercato globale che ogni anno assorbe circa 85 milioni di auto (settanta se si escludono gli Stati Uniti, un mercato praticamente inaccessibile ai cinesi).

Di fronte al calo della domanda interna, alle aziende cinesi restano due scelte, aggiunge il Wall Street Journal: da un lato riducono i prezzi per accaparrarsi una fetta del mercato interno (dall’inizio del 2023 i prezzi dei veicoli cinesi sono diminuiti di quasi il 20 per cento); dall’altro puntano sulle esportazioni (quest’anno la Cina dovrebbe vendere all’estero dodici milioni di auto, all’inizio del decennio in corso le vendite annuali si aggiravano sul milione), sfruttando tra l’altro uno yuan perennemente svalutato da Pechino.

Ora la Cina comincia ad accorgersi che questa strategia non può continuare a lungo: all’interno i prezzi non possono scendere ulteriormente; all’estero gli altri paesi cominciano a reagire all’ondata di auto cinesi, che sta mettendo in ginocchio le loro aziende. Insomma, addossare al resto del mondo i punti deboli della propria economia non è la soluzione.

Il problema è che il presidente Xi Jinping non sembra avere il pieno controllo della situazione, soprattutto perché molte amministrazioni locali invischiate nel settore automobilistico non hanno intenzione di staccare la spina alle aziende, sia perché temono di perdere tanti posti di lavoro sia perché vedrebbero ridursi le loro entrate fiscali, danneggiando ulteriormente finanze già messe a dura prova dall’esplosione della bolla immobiliare.

La spirale del debito

La Cina, lanciata da Xi Jinping in grandiosi progetti legati alle tecnologie militari e civili più avanzate (dai pannelli solari all’intelligenza artificiale), è finita in una pericolosa spirale del debito: nel 2025 i prestiti concessi a settori non finanziari – grandi conglomerati industriali, enti pubblici e famiglie – hanno raggiunto il 300 per cento del pil nazionale, 60 punti percentuali in più rispetto alla fine del 2019 e 43mila miliardi di dollari in più del 2012, cioè da quando Xi è arrivato al potere. Molto di questo denaro è stato buttato prima in immobili che oggi non vuole nessuno e poi in fabbriche che perdono soldi perché non trovano abbastanza acquirenti e non possono più di tanto abbassare i prezzi o decurtare i salari degli operai.

L’enorme mole di debiti e attività in perdita forse non provocherà una crisi finanziaria in un paese come la Cina, ma di sicuro ne sta indebolendo l’economia. Le prospettive rosee suscitate dalla straordinaria crescita degli ultimi decenni stanno lasciando il posto al pessimismo: quello di molti giovani, che fanno fatica a trovare occupazioni adeguate alle loro competenze; e quello di molti lavoratori che, tagliati fuori dall’automazione, ormai si riciclano nel mondo precario della gig economy (quest’anno il numero dei cosiddetti gig worker cinesi dovrebbe arrivare a 320 milioni, contro i 280 milioni del 2025).

Xi forse pensa che tutto si possa risolvere quando la Cina si affermerà come una potenza globale del livello degli Stati Uniti, se non superiore a loro. Anche per questo continua a ignorare gli appelli di molti economisti – cinesi e non – che consigliano di far crescere i consumi interni: questa svolta darebbe respiro sia alle aziende in cerca di clienti sia ai lavoratori, oltre a creare nuove entrate per lo stato e le amministrazioni locali; ne sarebbero felici anche gli altri paesi, alle prese con l’ondata di esportazioni cinesi.

Tuttavia, aumentare i consumi interni ridurrebbe la presa di Pechino sull’economia nazionale e distoglierebbe capitali da settori che Xi giudica strategici. Intanto, per aiutare le finanze pubbliche Pechino ha lanciato una vasta campagna contro l’evasione e l’elusione fiscale dei ricchi cinesi. Ma come osservano gli economisti Navneeraj Sharma e Arvind Subramanian, a questo punto “è probabile che si verifichi un lento declino caratterizzato da una crescita anemica, un crescente malcontento e un deterioramento dei servizi”. Comunque sufficiente per avere ripercussioni sull’intera economia globale.

articles.title: Japan eyes early contribution payment to ICC as court faces U.S. sanctions
articles.summary: If the sanctions are fully implemented as early as April next year, the ICC could be cut off from dollar-based settlements.
articles.preview: Tokyo is considering paying its 2027 contributions to the International Criminal Court ahead of schedule, in light of U.S. sanctions against the ICC, government sources have said. In October, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump designated the ICC for sanctions, giving a 180-day moratorium. It had already announced sanctions on ICC President Tomoko Akane in August.
articles.body:
Tokyo is considering paying its 2027 contributions to the International Criminal Court ahead of schedule, in light of U.S. sanctions against the ICC, government sources have said.

In October, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump designated the ICC for sanctions, giving a 180-day moratorium. It had already announced sanctions on ICC President Tomoko Akane in August.

If the sanctions are fully implemented as early as April next year, the ICC could be cut off from dollar-based settlements, potentially disrupting its operations, including staff salary payments.

“If nothing is done, the ICC could soon face a funding shortfall,” a Japanese government official said Friday.

Tokyo has paid its annual contributions to the ICC after April each year, based on its new fiscal-year budget.

If the government decides to make an advance payment for 2027, it could include the necessary funds in a second supplementary budget for fiscal 2026.

The ICC’s 2026 budget totals about €196 million, or about ¥34.5 billion. Japan contributed about ¥4.6 billion this year, the largest amount by a single country.

Akane, a Japanese national, has requested early contributions from her home country.

“We will consider what financial measures we can take while continuing to communicate with President Akane and relevant countries,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a news conference Thursday.

articles.body:
Di tutte le sfide che l’Europa deve affrontare, ce n’è una che non avevamo previsto: quella dei giovani. Potevamo aspettarci che la generazione Z si ribellasse in Nepal, in Marocco o anche in Serbia, ma nelle democrazie liberali dell’Unione europea? Le classi dirigenti e i mezzi d’informazione sono in allerta per il rischio di una possibile guerra; sono consapevoli dei problemi strutturali dell’economia europea (segnalati, tra gli altri, nel rapporto Draghi); si interrogano sulla dipendenza nei confronti di un’amministrazione statunitense che volta decisamente le spalle al vecchio (molto vecchio) continente; si occupano perfino di crisi climatica. Ma i giovani?

Tutti questi problemi li coinvolgono, ma non ne sono chiaramente il fulcro. Anche se ragazze e ragazzi si preoccupano della guerra, della tecnologia, del clima e dello stato del mondo, raramente trovano un discorso politico rivolto direttamente a loro. Come se non bastasse, l’Europa, dopo essere apparsa a lungo come “l’unica utopia ragionevole possibile” (secondo la fortunata definizione dello scrittore spagnolo Javier Cercas) ha perso la capacità di far sognare.

L’Erasmus, la libera circolazione nel continente europeo (malgrado le tensioni ricorrenti) e la moneta comune, che appare ancora miracolosa a tutti quelli che hanno conosciuto le valute nazionali, non hanno lo stesso peso per chi non ha vissuto queste rivoluzioni. Qual è l’ultimo, grande progetto europeo che potrebbe motivare chi ha 18 anni? Il pilastro europeo della Nato?

In quest’epoca ansiogena, in cui i rischi geopolitici si aggiungono alla crisi climatica e alle incertezze legate alla tecnologia, possiamo credere davvero che l’Europa sia ancora capace di convincere una nuova generazione? L’esempio britannico dimostra che l’errore della Brexit è stato pagato caro: i giovani britannici, senza più la possibilità di partecipare ai programmi comuni dell’Unione, sono stati fortemente penalizzati e oggi sono il motivo per cui il Partito laburista vorrebbe riportare il paese nell’Unione europea.

Eppure, nel continente, l’Unione affronta un paradosso enorme: tutti i sondaggi d’opinione indicano un forte legame tra la popolazione e il progetto europeo, ma i partiti in crescita sono apertamente euroscettici o decisi a scontrarsi con Bruxelles per perseguire i loro obiettivi.

Questo significa che il futuro dell’Unione e le minacce esterne passano in secondo piano rispetto alla rabbia o alle preoccupazioni quotidiane. I leader europei, a Bruxelles e nelle altre capitali, non danno l’impressione di aver colto questa spaccatura che contiene in sé il germe della distruzione del progetto europeo.

Oppure, se ne sono consapevoli, non hanno risposte da fornire a ragazze e ragazzi, che sentono di non avere un futuro e reagiscono rumorosamente, confusamente e a volte violentemente. La vera sfida europea del momento, dunque, è più complessa del previsto: come fare a proteggere l’Unione in un mondo diventato più pericoloso a causa del risveglio degli imperi e allo stesso tempo restituire un orizzonte ai giovani, che non sono disposti a sacrificare il loro presente e il loro futuro per questioni che potrebbero sembrare lontane? Bisogna fare in fretta, la casa sta già bruciando.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

articles.title: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
articles.summary: Santiago Peña was ousted due to a banking crisis which left millions of people unable to access their money.
articles.preview: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private business interests. Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office due to a widening crisis triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this week. He had offered to step down on Thursday.
articles.body:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private business interests.

Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office due to a widening crisis triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this week.

He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.

Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.

The demise of the digital bank has left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.

An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions prompting widespread protests particularly in the capital, Asunción.

The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.

Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.

Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".

Paraguay's Vice-President Pedro Alliana was then sworn in as interim President.

"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as President until 2028.

Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history â a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."

Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.

His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

In an address to the nation on Thursday, Peña said that he was sorry and that "it was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me".

articles.title: China's giant pandas make public debut at US zoo
articles.summary: Giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will make Zoo Atlanta home for the next 10 years.
articles.preview: Giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will make Zoo Atlanta home for the next 10 years. ATLANTA: Giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang delighted visitors to Zoo Atlanta during their public debut Friday (Nov 6), chewing bamboo and lounging in their new US habitat while on loan from China. A male named Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang arrived from Chengdu in September via a FedEx flight dubbed the "Panda Express", and are to be hosted in the southern US facility for the next 10 years.
articles.body:
Giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will make Zoo Atlanta home for the next 10 years.

ATLANTA: Giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang delighted visitors to Zoo Atlanta during their public debut Friday (Nov 6), chewing bamboo and lounging in their new US habitat while on loan from China.

A male named Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang arrived from Chengdu in September via a FedEx flight dubbed the "Panda Express", and are to be hosted in the southern US facility for the next 10 years.

Pandas are "animals that have got a unique ability to inspire curiosity, instil passion, evoke joy, and unite people around the globe", CEO Raymond King told onlookers at Zoo Atlanta.

"This extraordinary spirit of partnership helps create a future for a species that is truly beloved the world over."

In preparation for their arrival, Zoo Atlanta has renovated its panda facilities and assembled a team of animal caretakers.

It has also ensured a stable and long-term supply of bamboo, grown locally in Atlanta, which has a climate that is very similar to Chengdu.

"I think they inspire happiness," zoo visitor Rachel Totts told AFP on Friday. "They make people smile. I've never seen someone not say 'Oh, it's so cute!' when they're looking at a panda."

Native to temperate forest habitats in East Asia, the lumbering black-and-white mammals do not typically travel long distances in the wild.

But many have been shipped to zoos around the world as part of Beijing's decades-long "panda diplomacy" programme to foster foreign ties.

The furry show of "soft power" came as top US officials on Friday called on China to uphold the trade agreement made in an October 2025 meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping.

The accord calmed tensions after a whirlwind of tariff hikes, and required China to buy US soybeans while suspending export controls on rare earths.

Before 2016, pandas were considered endangered but are now listed as "vulnerable" by wildlife advocates, and an estimated 1,800 pandas live in the wild.

The Chinese government has established more than 50 panda reserves for conservation, but in the wild the bears continue to face threats of habitat loss and poaching.

Atlanta previously hosted pandas on loan from China starting in 1999, and seven panda cubs have been born at the zoo. All are now back in Chengdu, and Zoo Atlanta has not had any pandas since 2024.

Both of the new arrivals were born in 2020, and it's hoped they will be suitable mates. Pandas in captivity typically live for around 30 years.

In 1972, China gifted a pair of pandas to Washington, following US President Richard Nixon's historic visit to the Communist nation.

Beijing recalled two of its pandas from Japan early this year, following a diplomatic spat that began when Japan's prime minister hinted that Tokyo could intervene militarily in the event of any attack on Taiwan.

articles.title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
articles.summary: The US president's promotion of Miller, a loyal partisan firebrand to be his new chief of staff sets up likely clashes with Congress.
articles.preview: In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress. On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.
articles.body:
In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.

On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.

"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.

One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.

"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."

Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.

He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.

He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.

Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.

He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.

Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.

The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.

- Published9 February

Miller's hardline views sets up clash with Congress

While Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.

It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats â and some Republicans.

"Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X. "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."

Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".

The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.

Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.

On Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-president JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement- by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance".

That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.

Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".

Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises.

"Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.

At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.

articles.body:
Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran to allow UN nuclear weapons inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites, including those housing the country’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran would not be required to make any commitment that the stockpile would be removed from the country, with other options on the table, including reducing the uranium content by down-blending it.

Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents.

The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”.

Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms.

Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.

Iran would open the strait of Hormuz on the second day, via a route it has already negotiated with Oman that they would jointly lodge with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

Iran has multiple other preconditions for opening the strait including ending the war in Lebanon, a withdrawal of US forces from the Iranian coastline, a commitment to lift some economic sanctions, and agreement to pay war reparations. The sequencing of these commitments has been at the heart of the mediation.

In the memorandum of understanding, a $300bn reconstruction and development fund was to be set up to help Iran recover economically, but it was never clear exactly how this proposal was to be funded.

Iran, in a triumphalist mood after Trump’s election wipeout, has been wary of allowing the UN nuclear inspectors back into the country, claiming it had lost faith in Rafael Grossi, the head of the inspectorate.

Tehran claims Grossi betrayed his duty to uphold the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, by failing to criticise the US for bombing Iran’s nuclear sites. It fears that material gathered by the inspectors would be handed over as targeting data to the Americans and Israelis.

In the parallel talks on opening the strait, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, spoke again to Iran about the future of the strait administration including the agreed route, the extent to which the agreement is temporary and the need to register the proposal with the IMO, either as a bilateral agreement or a joint regional proposal.

Oman has a long-term proposal for the administration of the strait compliant with the law of the sea in that shipping companies would be charged only for services, and not tolls.

Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chair of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) on Tuesday that ships from four countries – China, India, Qatar and Iraq – were allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.

The exemptions served mutual interests, he said, adding that Iran charged Indian and Chinese vessels transit fees while allowing Qatari ships to pass free of charge. Medicine was received from India, while China provided political support.

It is reported that of the 10.23m barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42% went to China and 13% to India, said Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler.

The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two “violating” oil tankers attempting to pass through an unauthorised route in the eastern sector of the strait of Hormuz had collided with mines and caught fire.

The IRGC said the two tankers had turned off their navigation and identification systems and that the attempted crossing was with the support of US military forces.

L'esercito iraniano ha affermato oggi di essere "più forte" rispetto all'inizio della guerra in Medio Oriente, dichiarandosi pronto a rispondere a qualsiasi attacco in modo 'immediato' e "senza limiti geografici" a seguito delle recenti minacce statunitensi.

"Le forze armate della Repubblica islamica sono oggi in uno stato di allerta più elevato e sono più potenti di quanto non fossero all'inizio della guerra", ha dichiarato il portavoce dell'esercito, Mohammad Akraminia, citato dall'agenzia ufficiale Irna. "Su ordine della Guida Suprema, qualsiasi risposta delle forze armate sarà immediata, efficace e senza limiti geografici", ha aggiunto.

Nonostante i recenti attacchi statunitensi sull'isola di Qeshm, nello stretto di Hormuz, le trattative diplomatiche per evitare una ripresa delle ostilità si sono recentemente intensificate con la mediazione del Qatar, dopo una serie di minacce israelo-statunitensi.

L'agenzia di stampa semi-ufficiale iraniana Tasnim ha riferito che, secondo le prime segnalazioni, due missili avrebbero colpito l'isola di Qeshm, aggiungendo che non vi sono informazioni ufficiali su eventuali danni.

In precedenza, l'agenzia di stampa statale Irna aveva riportato la testimonianza di persone del luogo, secondo le quali due proiettili avrebbero colpito l'area di Suza, sull'isola di Qeshm, nel sud dell'Iran, dopo che era stato udito il rumore di un velivolo sopra l'isola.

"Non voglio parlarne. Abbiamo condotto un piccolo attacco in Iran. Hanno costruito un piccolo dispositivo antiaereo e lo abbiamo messo fuori combattimento in 15 minuti, forse cinque", ha detto Donald Trump, rispondendo a chi gli chiedeva se gli Stati Uniti fossero stati dietro l'attacco.

L'amministrazione Trump è spaccata sull'Iran. Il vicepresidente JD Vance preme per la fine del conflitto, mentre il capo del Pentagono Pete Hegseth e il numero uno dell'Us Central Command Brad Cooper spingono per un ritorno ai combattimenti. Lo riporta il Wall Street Journal citando alcune fonti, secondo le quali le tensioni fra le varie posizioni all'interno dell'amministrazione si sono intensificate dopo la elezioni di metà mandato.

I segretari di Stato Marco Rubio e del Tesoro Scott Bessent spingono invece per un inasprimento delle sanzioni e per proseguire il blocco. L'inviato Steve Witkoff sostiene la posizione di Vance. Il premier israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu vorrebbe una ripresa dei combattimenti. Gli Stati Uniti offrono 20 milioni di dollari, "oltre alla possibilità di trasferirsi altrove", a chiunque fornisca informazioni sul programma nucleare iraniano. Tali informazioni possono riguardare "le sue strutture, le sue attrezzature e il personale a esse associato", ha detto lo Us Central Command.

articles.title: 'It would facilitate Gaza genocide': Protesters storm Microsoft planned site
articles.summary: 'It would facilitate Gaza genocide': Protesters storm Microsoft planned site Several hundred activists occupied the construction site of a planned Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam on Friday, protesting the technology giant's alleged role in facilitating Israel's genocide in Gaza, as well as the environmental impact of artificial intelligence infrastructure. The demonstration, organised by climate and justice collective Geef Tegengas and environmental group Fossielvrij, halted construction work for the day in the city's Sloterdijk district. The protesters argued that the facility could be used to support AI-powered warfare and Israel's military operations in Gaza. "It's so many things, so many struggles that come together in this data centre," Nathan Timmer, a spokesman for Geef Tegengas, told AFP. Timmer, 30, accused the project of helping to facilitate "AI warfare" and what he described as the "genocide" in Gaza. Dutch news agency ANP reported that police arrested between 150 and 200 protesters, while others left voluntarily. The protest was part of a wider two-day mobilisation across Europe called by the Stop Dirty Data Centers coalition, which is demanding a pause in the construction of new data centre facilities. Report by AFP Dutch police officers detain a demonstrator during a protest by the Geef Tegengas group against the construction of a Microsoft data centre in Sloterdijk, near Amsterdam on 6 November 2026. (AFP)
