Nella notte tra il 6 e il 7 novembre, diverse ondate di missili balistici russi hanno colpito Kiev, poche ore dopo che il presidente Volodymyr Zelensky aveva avvertito che la Russia si stava preparando a un altro attacco su larga scala contro le infrastrutture. Lo riferisce The Kyiv Independent.

Almeno cinque persone sono rimaste ferite nella capitale, tra cui una ragazza di 14 anni, secondo quanto riferito dal sindaco Vitali Klitschko. Il Ponte Nord di Kiev è stato danneggiato nell'attacco russo ed è stato chiuso al traffico in entrambe le direzioni, ha aggiunto Klitschko. Gli attacchi russi hanno danneggiato impianti energetici nella regione di Kiev, oltre a un ponte fondamentale nella capitale ucraina. Lo ha confermato il sindaco della città.

"A seguito di un attacco nemico avvenuto durante la notte, sono stati danneggiati impianti energetici nelle regioni di Kiev e di Žytomyr. La situazione relativa all'approvvigionamento energetico della capitale è estremamente difficile", ha scritto su Telegram il sindaco Vitali Klitschko. "Anche il Ponte del Nord è stato danneggiato in un attacco nemico. Gli specialisti stanno valutando l'entità dei danni", ha aggiunto Klitschko in un altro messaggio su Telegram.

L'Ucraina ha intanto colpito nella stessa notte diversi siti nelle regioni russe di Oryol, Saratov e Rostov, tra cui una raffineria di petrolio. Lo riferisce The Kyiv Independent. Secondo quanto riportato dal canale di monitoraggio Exilenova Plus, nella raffineria di petrolio di Saratov è scoppiato un incendio dopo un attacco ucraino con droni. S

articles.title: How the Iran war helped Democrats win the midterms
articles.summary: Tehran brought the costs of war into American homes, fuelling the backlash against Trump's party.
articles.preview: Trump sought to bring Iran to its knees. Instead, Tehran brought the costs of war into American homes, fuelling the backlash against his party. This week, Iran’s response to the US-Israeli attacks led to one of the most dramatic political turnarounds in modern American history. Trump’s failed war on its own, however, is not why the Democrats pounded the Republicans and now control the Senate and House of Representatives for the next two years.
articles.body:
Trump sought to bring Iran to its knees. Instead, Tehran brought the costs of war into American homes, fuelling the backlash against his party.

This week, Iran’s response to the US-Israeli attacks led to one of the most dramatic political turnarounds in modern American history. Trump’s failed war on its own, however, is not why the Democrats pounded the Republicans and now control the Senate and House of Representatives for the next two years. Rather, it reflected and amplified many dynamics in American society that caused discontented, angry and fearful citizens to repudiate Trump’s Republicans and support Democrats.

The US president wrongly believed that his war on Iran would pummel the country into submission and turn it into a vassal state of the US and Israel. Iran survived, attacked the US, Israel and Arab lands, and brought the painful economic costs of war into every American home. It also humiliated Washington by revealing that America’s military prowess, like Trump’s behaviour and electoral promises, is erratic at best, and ineffective at worst.

The Iran war also sparked a cascade of consequences that hurt every American and, in some areas, exposed how national values such as democracy, equality and the rule of law, along with claims of global dominance, could prove illusory. Iran’s move with the greatest impact on ordinary Americans was restricting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up the prices Americans paid for groceries, gasoline, diesel, travel, most imports and other everyday necessities. Some 90 percent of voters said the cost of living was a major or crucial factor in how they would vote.

This was compounded by the inability of the US and Israel to force Iran to surrender, even after months of brutal attacks on political leaders, infrastructure, civilian and economic sites, and military installations. Instead, Iran’s counterattacks left US bases in the Arabian Peninsula and Jordan incapacitated or evacuated, and caused huge damage to Arab energy and transport systems, disrupting global energy flows and driving up prices. The balance of the war was clear after the first few weeks: the pain the US and Israel inflicted on Iran would be matched by pain in every household in the US and other countries that assisted in the attack on Iran.

Iran simultaneously exposed critical flaws in American militarism, leaving ordinary Americans confused, frustrated and often humiliated in different ways:

a) Trump ignored Americans’ repeatedly expressed opposition to attacking Iran, along with the constitutional requirement for congressional authorisation of war. CBS exit polls confirmed that voters opposed the war for both its useless militarism and its impact on the economy. The Trump administration’s disdain for both the law and ordinary Americans’ views angered many voters who took their constitutional rights more seriously than Trump did. Many voters rejected Republicans because Trump had insincerely promised in 2024 that he would end useless foreign wars.

b) More narrowly, Trump attacked Iran without clear, consistent or credible strategic goals; his main stated reason for attacking was to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, a prospect Israeli officials repeatedly told him was imminent, even though existing US and international inspections and intelligence assessments had repeatedly found no evidence of this.

c) When it dawned on Americans that Trump went to war mainly because Israel pushed him to do so, they reacted negatively in two ways. They felt humiliated that their country’s immense military power was unable to achieve its stated goals; they also felt angry and demeaned that a small, dependent, foreign country like Israel, with its extensive and sophisticated lobbying power in the US, could initiate this calamity that hurt American households and damaged US standing and credibility abroad.

Behind the anger, vulnerability and helplessness of most Americans who voted Democratic this week were deeper grievances that predated the Iran war. These included citizens’ fury at outrageous corruption in Washington; the privileged oligarchs, political donors, bankers and corporations that saw the US as their personal profit centre more than anything else; military and high-tech sectors that were out of control and threatened innocent lives; over-aggressive anti-immigration policing; and corporate media that seemed more interested in serving all of the above, and Israel, than in conveying truth and facts to the American people.

The election brought together voters’ household economic concerns with questions of national morality and foreign policy. Equally noteworthy, the day after the vote, Vice President JD Vance wrote on social media: “The reason we lost is the war.” He identified four demands among voters who had turned away from the Republicans: “End the war”, “Focus on the cost of living and inflation”, “Put America First” and “Change our relationship to Israel”.

An unprecedented aspect of this election and Iran’s policies has been the centrality of the US-Israeli genocide in Palestine to many progressive Democrats’ campaigns and to Iran’s approach to war and peace. Vance’s explicit mention of Israel was startling enough in a political system that, for nearly a century, has largely shaped its West Asia policies according to Israeli demands. Equally striking was President Trump’s last-minute promise, on election day, to end the nearly $4bn in US military aid to Israel. It was another insincere Trump con job meant to deceive voters, because the money would not stop flowing but would simply be channelled differently. It also emphasised the huge impact that conditions in Israel-Palestine and US complicity in the genocide had on voters.

articles.body:
Missile attacks damage a residential building and injure civilians after Zelenskyy warns of potential for new strikes.

Russian forces have launched a missile attack on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor said, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned in his nightly video address that Russia was preparing new attacks on energy targets, bridges and other infrastructure.

Debris from Saturday’s attack damaged a residential building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

“Explosions in the Kyiv suburbs. The enemy is hitting infrastructure with ballistic missiles,” Klitschko wrote on Telegram.

Klitschko said debris had struck a five-storey apartment building in a western district of the capital. The facade of another residential building was also damaged.

The city’s military administration said on Telegram that two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was damaged.

Officials continued to warn residents of the potential for more strikes hours after the attack.

The attacks come as Zelenskyy said his government is seeking specific guarantees from Western allies on how post-war security support would function. He made comments in an interview aired late on Thursday, following two days of discussions among allies in Brussels.

The talks in Brussels discussed post-war reconstruction, funding for next year and security guarantees backed by the Ukrainian government’s Western allies.

The meetings brought together officials from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and the European Union, along with representatives from the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock, Ukrainian lead negotiator Rustem Umerov wrote in an online post.

US-led talks

The attacks occurred three days before US-led Ukrainian-Russian talks were to open in Abu Dhabi seeking a resolution to the war that has gone on for more than four years. The last such talks took place in February.

On Thursday, US President Donald Trump said a deal between Russia and Ukraine may be imminent, following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, at the White House.

Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.

The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came on the same day as First Lady Melania Trump hosted a diplomatic gathering with Russian and Ukrainian representatives to mark and build on a localised truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October.

The truce expired last Sunday, a day before a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhia region.

The death toll from the attack has risen to 50, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said on Friday, making it one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year.

articles.title: Israeli settler attacks on West Bank olive harvest hit record since 2006, UN says
articles.summary: Israeli settler attacks on West Bank olive harvest hit record since 2006, UN says The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has said Israeli settlers have carried out a total of 377 attacks on olive harvest across the occupied West Bank since September, a record since 2006 when the UN began recording them. In a statement, OCHA said that during these attacks, one Palestinian was killed by a settler, more than 200 Palestinians were injured, and over 3,850 olive trees and saplings were damaged or vandalised. Combined with official Israeli restrictions on Palestinian access to groves, this has undermined the livelihoods of many by reducing the produce that Palestinians could collect, the statement read. Food security partners estimate that 80,000 to 100,000 Palestinian families across the West Bank depend on the annual olive harvest for their livelihoods and income. * Gaza : OCHA said restrictions continue to hamper aid to Gaza despite widespread humanitarian response. Humanitarian partners warn that the entry of engine oil, spare parts, generators, heavy machinery and specialised equipment remain particularly restricted. This prevents the implementation of more sustainable shelter solutions and risks shutting down critical services if back-up generators fail, according to the statement. The attacks have resulted in the death of a Palestinian and injury to 200 others. (AFP)

articles.summary: The president’s announcement comes days after an earlier attack on Iran was made public, and as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have accelerated Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.” Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February. articles.preview: The president’s announcement comes days after an earlier attack on Iran was made public, and as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have accelerated Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.” Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in…
articles.body:
Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”

Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.

In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”.

The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.

Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.

The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy.

In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.

Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.

US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the US was offering “a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.

The post included a link to the state department’s Rewards for Justice program.

Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators’ discussions with Iran continue.

“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump.

A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the US military to carry out new strikes against Iran.

US defense secretary Pete Hegseth spoke on Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. Qatar has been mediating between the US and Iran to end the war.

The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defence officials after confirming earlier that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.

The telephone call between Trump and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani focused on international efforts to end tensions, according to a statement from the Qatari ruler’s media office.

With the Associated Press

articles.body:
Ben Roberts-Smith has collaborated with a gym supplements company run by a rightwing influencer which recently sold a pre-workout product called “war crimes”.

Roberts-Smith, one of Australia’s most decorated living soldiers who is currently awaiting trial on war crimes charges, has recently launched an apparel brand, Epic 1 Two, producing T-shirts and gym wear.

In October, he also appeared in a social media video collaboration between his brand and Zero Limits supplements, co-owned by the rightwing podcaster and fitness coach Chris Katelaris, also known as “Big Chocky”.

Roberts-Smith, Katelaris and others were filmed during a gym workout, with on-screen graphics reading “Zero Limits Supplements x Epic 1 Two”. Both brands were labelled “collaborators” on the video, which is also published on the Instagram grids of both brands.

Months earlier, Zero Limits had repeatedly posted online about a product titled “war crimes”, an energy supplement in the flavour “kill or capture cola”. Its label depicted a hooded captive on a chair in a room with an Australian flag on the wall, and a tall figure wearing a balaclava and military-style clothing.

In a video on 26 July, Katelaris promoted the product while holding a tub at the gym.

“You wanna drink out of a prosthetic leg? You wanna re-enact a Sparta kick? You wanna execute your workout?” he said.

“War crimes, it’s the pre-workout for you.”

Zero Limits, which says it is “veteran owned and operated”, does not currently list the “war crimes” product on its website, and Roberts-Smith is not shown endorsing, referencing or using that particular product.

The former soldier has praised another product from Zero Limits, posting an Instagram story – since shared by the brand – from Epic 1 Two’s Instagram page of himself drinking a separate pre-workout drink.

Roberts-Smith gave the brand a “massive shout out” and told followers to “get on their website and take a look”, sharing a link to its website. Roberts-Smith also last week appeared on the Zero Limits podcast, hosted by another founder of the supplements company of the same name.

Roberts-Smith was in April arrested and charged with five counts of war crime – murder, in relation to three incidents stemming from his service in Afghanistan in 2009 and 2012.

He has denied the charges, saying in a statement after his arrest: “As I’ve always maintained: I categorically deny all of these allegations … I will be taking this opportunity to finally clear my name. I’m proud of my service in Afghanistan.”

The three incidents allegedly involved Afghan nationals being shot dead by Roberts-Smith, or a subordinate under his command, while he was present, the AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said in April.

Roberts-Smith was previously found in a defamation suit – using the civil standard of the balance of probabilities – to have murdered unarmed civilians while serving in the Australian Special Air Service Regiment (SAS) in Afghanistan.

The federal court found to the lower civil standard that Roberts-Smith kicked Afghan man Ali Jan in the chest, sending him falling backwards over a cliff before he landed on the ground. The court found that Roberts-Smith then ordered another soldier to shoot him dead.

Roberts-Smith was also accused in media reporting of shooting an unarmed prisoner who had a prosthetic leg. The leg was later used as a drinking vessel by soldiers.

Zero Limits, Katelaris and Roberts-Smith were contacted for comment.

In a statement via a lawyer, Zero Limits did not respond to specific questions, only answering: “The products are great, make sure you check them out.”

In a statement via the same lawyer, Katelaris also did not respond to specific questions, but said: “If you thought this was wild, wait until next week’s campaign drops.”

Katelaris lists himself as a “co-owner” of the supplements brand in his Instagram bio. He also promotes a range of merchandise under his own name in support of Roberts-Smith, including “I stand with BRS” T-shirts, hats, hoodies and stubby coolers.

articles.body:
European nations want Russia to halt its war against Ukraine before entertaining any talk of the Kremlin’s concerns about the continent’s broader security architecture, people familiar with the matter said, a stance that risks putting them at odds with the U.S. over the best way to end the conflict.

European officials are also adamant that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s pre-war demands that would effectively roll back NATO’s presence in Eastern Europe are still unacceptable, said the people, who asked not to be identified to discuss private deliberations.

One of the main goals of the existing security framework is to deter Russia from attacking Europe. It would make little sense to have such discussions while Moscow continues to wage war against Ukraine and is violating an array of existing agreements, some of the people said.

articles.preview: Around 100 demonstrators entered the site in the Sloterdijk district, although organisers claimed several hundred had taken part. Activists used ladders to scale the perimeter fence and cut an opening to allow others inside. Some climbed a construction crane, displaying a banner reading "Fuck AI", while others waved Palestinian flags and held signs accusing Microsoft of supporting genocide. Police surrounded the protesters before the mayor ordered the demonstration to end. Riot officers subsequently intervened, with several arrests reported. The protest was organised by Dutch activist collective Geef Tegengas, alongside a separate mobilisation by environmental campaign group Fossielvrij NL. Campaigners oppose the development over its expected electricity consumption, its impact on housing plans and concerns about Microsoft's activities. The project, developed by Pure Data Centres for Microsoft, involves three towers approximately 85 metres high, with an investment exceeding $1 billion. Protesters argue that the facilities could consume as much electricity as all Amsterdam households combined, a claim that has not been independently established. The action formed part of an international campaign against large-scale data centres, with demonstrations planned across several European countries. Both Pure Data Centres and Microsoft said they respected peaceful protest, while urging demonstrators to avoid unlawful actions.

articles.title: I pm possono procedere su Giusi Bartolozzi per false dichiarazioni

Ma per l'ex capo di gabinetto del ministero della Giustizia al momento il bicchiere è mezzo vuoto: secondo la Corte costituzionale, i magistrati di piazzale Clodio possono procedere, ma dovranno prima informare la Camera, in merito alle indagini che vedono la ex dirigente di via Arenula accusata di false dichiarazioni al pm sul caso del generale libico Almasri, che fu arrestato a Torino e poi…
articles.body:
La Consulta accoglie parzialmente il ricorso della Camera nei confronti del Tribunale dei ministri e della Procura di Roma sulla posizione di Giusi Bartolozzi. Ma per l'ex capo di gabinetto del ministero della Giustizia al momento il bicchiere è mezzo vuoto: secondo la Corte costituzionale, i magistrati di piazzale Clodio possono procedere, ma dovranno prima informare la Camera, in merito alle indagini che vedono la ex dirigente di via Arenula accusata di false dichiarazioni al pm sul caso del generale libico Almasri, che fu arrestato a Torino e poi rilasciato e riportato con un aereo dei servizi a Tripoli.

Ma la questione giuridica, che va avanti a colpi di istanze, non sembra affatto conclusa: l'obbligo per la Procura di dare comunicazione alla Camera sull'indagine nei confronti di Bartolozzi potrebbe aprire ad un nuovo ricorso alla Consulta, visto che l'assemblea dei deputati a questo punto ha la facoltà di sollevare l'ennesimo conflitto di attribuzione di fronte ai giudici della Corte. E la sentenza della Corte, di fatto interlocutoria, disegna uno scenario ancora incerto, che non si esaurisce solo all'indagine per l'accusa di false dichiarazioni. Oltre a questo reato, 'connesso' a quelli di cui era accusato il Guardasigilli Carlo Nordio, resta la questione sui presunti reati 'in concorso' con il ministro, per i quali è stata invece negata l'autorizzazione a procedere assieme ad altri vertici del governo (nello specifico, omissione di atti d'ufficio e concorso in favoreggiamento personale aggravato).

La Camera dei deputati aveva fatto ricorso contro i magistrati romani proprio perché avrebbero dovuto chiedere anche per Bartolozzi l'autorizzazione a procedere, per il ruolo da lei rivestito all'epoca al ministero. Con la sentenza di oggi la Consulta risponde che, laddove avesse configurato un tale 'concorso', il Tribunale avrebbe dovuto in quel caso chiedere alla Camera l'autorizzazione a procedere anche nei confronti della stessa Bartolozzi, oltre che del ministro. La Corte ha infatti rilevato che, "all'esito delle indagini svolte dal Tribunale nei confronti del ministro, la Procura aveva espressamente invitato il Tribunale a qualificare la condotta di Bartolozzi come concorso nei reati ascritti al ministro Nordio, o, alternativamente, a ipotizzare a suo carico il reato di false dichiarazioni durante le indagini. In virtù del principio di leale collaborazione tra i poteri dello Stato, a fronte di questa sollecitazione, il Tribunale avrebbe dovuto esplicitare le ragioni per le quali non ha ritenuto di configurare, in capo a Bartolozzi, una possibile responsabilità per concorso nei reati attribuiti al ministro".

Sul reato di false dichiarazioni al pm di cui Bartolozzi è accusata, restano poi da sciogliere dei nodi. Se i magistrati procedono per un altro reato, potevano sentire la ex capo di gabinetto solo come 'persona informata sui fatti' e quindi senza un avvocato? Da questo punto di vista c'è chi non esclude al momento anche un ricorso per la lesione dei diritti di difesa di Bartolozzi. E per la ex dirigente di via Arenula, alle beghe giudiziarie personali, in queste stesse ore si aggiungono anche quelle legate a suo marito Gaetano Armao, ex vicepresidente della Regione Sicilia, accusato di corruzione in tutt'altra vicenda: per lui il Gip di Palermo ha disposto gli arresti domiciliari sul caso delle autorizzazioni ambientali della regione.

articles.title: UN says struggling to help millions fleeing Sudan war find shelter
articles.summary: The United Nations on Friday said about 15.4 million people who have fled conflict in Sudan need emergency shelter and essential household items, but humanitarian organisations are facing funding shortages.
articles.preview: Sudan Millions of people who have fled devastating conflict in Sudan face being left without shelter, the United Nations warned Friday. After more than three years of civil war, the UN estimates that 15.4 million people need emergency shelter and essential household items. But UN agencies said they had only been able to target 10% of those in need because of funding shortages. And out of those, "we could reach only 900,000 people," said Mohamed Refaat, the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) chief of mission in Sudan.
articles.body:
Sudan

Millions of people who have fled devastating conflict in Sudan face being left without shelter, the United Nations warned Friday.

After more than three years of civil war, the UN estimates that 15.4 million people need emergency shelter and essential household items.

But UN agencies said they had only been able to target 10% of those in need because of funding shortages.

And out of those, "we could reach only 900,000 people," said Mohamed Refaat, the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) chief of mission in Sudan.

The war raging since April 2023 between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and the regular army has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, and has triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.

Around 8.6 million people remain displaced within the country, millions have fled across borders and millions more have returned home — often finding houses, infrastructure and essential services damaged or destroyed.

Since the start of the year, Refaat said the UN agency had distributed more than 40,000 tents.

"But our warehouses are completely empty now," he told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Khartoum.

"We could soon reach a point where families desperately need shelter but there is simply nothing left."

In a joint statement, UNHCR and IOM said for those returning home getting help to find shelter "is often the first step towards rebuilding their lives".

But only one third of the $179 million needed this year to provide shelter has so far been funded, Abubakarr Jalloh, UNHCR's deputy representative in Sudan, told reporters.

Three in four internally displaced people in Sudan are women and children, Jalloh said, adding that El Niño-related weather conditions have made people more vulnerable because of significantly below-average rainfall across Sudan this year.

This has affected harvests in Darfur, Kordofan and other areas already devastated by ongoing fighting. Although food prices would normally ease after the harvest season, prices remain “painfully high,” the UNHCR official said.

“For a family that has lost everything, every Sudanese pound spent on food is money that cannot be spent on a blanket or on materials needed for safe shelter,” Jalloh stressed.

The agencies said less than half of the $2.9 billion needed for the overall humanitarian aid plan for Sudan had been funded.

articles.title: UNICEF: Children at risk of disease and violence from rise in attacks on water systems
articles.summary: Children around the world are at greater risk from disease, malnutrition and violence due to a sharp rise in attacks on water and sanitation systems. Now UNICEF is calling on conflict parties, governments and humanitarian actors to treat those systems as life-saving civilian infrastructure.
articles.preview: Children around the world are at greater risk from disease, malnutrition and violence due to a sharp rise in attacks on water and sanitation systems. articles.body:
Water

Children around the world are at greater risk from disease, malnutrition and violence due to a sharp rise in attacks on water and sanitation systems. Now UNICEF is calling on conflict parties, governments and humanitarian actors to treat those systems as life-saving civilian infrastructure.

According to a new report from the UN Children's Agency, attacks that damaged or destroyed water and sanitation systems in conflict rose threefold between 2021 and 2025.

That deprives children of safe drinking water and exposes them to disease from poor sanitation. The report also documents how children in Gaza have been killed or injured while queuing for water.

Longer more dangerous journeys also raise their risk of sexual violence and take time away from school.

Efforts need to be made to guarantee humanitarian access so that water and energy supplies keep running, UNICEF says.

It also calls for the protection of those who operate and maintain water systems and for all attacks to be systematically documented.

articles.body:
Czech arms makers look spaceward in bid to sustain Ukraine-driven boom

November 6, 2026

Czech arms makers have thrived on demand linked to the war in Ukraine. To sustain their growth, they need to look beyond ammunition and toward new technologies — and even space.

The Czechoslovak Group (CSG) arms maker announced in mid-October that it has acquired a stake in Canadian space technology manufacturer MDA Space.

This space mission is part of the company's bid to continue riding the boom that has transformed its fortunes in recent years.

When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG soared to become the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe, with a market capitalization of €14.6 billion ($16.4 billion), propelling its owner, Michal Strnad, to the top of the region's rich list.

From 90s startup to major European player

CSG began life as a 1990s startup, selling military surplus amid the collapse of the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance between the Soviet Union and Europe's socialist Eastern Bloc nations, which was founded in 1955 and disbanded in 1991.

It has since grown to become the second-largest producer of ammunition in Europe after Germany's Rheinmetall and now produces across Europe and in the US.

The impact of the war in Ukraine

The main driver of the company's rising fortunes has been Russia's war in Ukraine, which has driven a dramatic boom across the Czech defense industry as a whole.

In 2021, the sector's exports totaled €600 million. In 2025, these exports had expanded to €4.7 billion, powered by orders placed by Kyiv and its European allies.

By the end of that year, European states had procured approximately €11 billion worth of military support for Ukraine from Czech defense firms.

Orders to the value of roughly €4 billion have arrived via the Czech Ammunition Initiative, a program that coordinates the transfer of artillery shells to Ukraine.

Amid the avalanche of orders sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, CSG and Czech peers such as STV, Colt CZ and PBS have been busy expanding production to pump out military vehicles and planes, guns, grenades, shells and bullets.

Historical link

"The war in Ukraine, particularly in its early stages, was especially well suited to Czech firms," Krzysytof Debiec of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) told DW.

Debiec says that this was largely due to the major role that the former Czechoslovakia played in supplying Warsaw Pact countries.

"Specialization in the production of ammunition — including Soviet calibers — the repair of Soviet-era equipment and the manufacture of relatively unsophisticated systems that could be rapidly introduced and were compatible with the Ukrainian army's existing stocks," have all been key, he explained.

At the same time, European states eyeing the threat from the east and broader geopolitical instability are boosting their own defense budgets.

"The shift in US policies vis-a-vis NATO is forcing European nations to increase their defense spending dramatically, and that's another factor" in the Czech defense industry boom, Jan Jires, a former deputy defense minister and now a senior advisor at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.

Export dependence

However, since launching on the stock exchange, CSG's share price has performed erratically, illustrating the shifting sands on which Czechia's booming defense industry now stands.

The government in Prague has responded to the sector's surge by transferring the defense industry portfolio from the Ministry of Defense to the Ministry of Industry and Trade to align its growing role in exports with national economic and trade policy.

At the same time, the populist ruling coalition that took power a year ago is made up of parties that have either promised to lower support for Ukraine or — in the case of the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) — are openly pro-Russian.

As a result, the coalition has halted contributions to the Czech Ammunition Initiative and is dragging its feet on raising defense spending to meet NATO targets.

This only limits an already small domestic market, leaving the industry dependent on exports for about 90% of its revenue — the vast bulk of which is still linked to Ukraine — and lacking a stable base for expansion.

"The Czech industry has outgrown the country's financial means," said Jires. "Unlike German, French or British companies, Czech manufacturers cannot rely on domestic demand to make them globally relevant."

What the future holds

Increased global defense spending looks set to continue, but an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, a change in US foreign policy or a calmer geopolitical environment would hit Czech arms manufacturers hard. For this reason, they must ponder what the future of war, and its funding, might look like.

The conflict in Ukraine offers some indicators, having become increasingly focused on swarms of drones and a technological race between Kyiv and Moscow to improve the performance of the unmanned aircraft.

Major questions must now be asked regarding "the size and role of the military, how it is equipped, what should be purchased and when new weaponry can arrive" Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.

For a company like CSG, for which bullets and shells currently account for around 60% of sales, these are vital questions.

"Czech companies — many of which still focus on relatively unsophisticated military production — must invest more in innovative manufacturing," said Debiec, who notes that most are well aware of the challenge. "They have reinvested their extraordinary profits and are already more technologically advanced and diversified in their production than they were in 2022."

Space mission

CSG's acquisition of MDA Space is part of such efforts.

The company, which already held interests in British and German space technology companies, pointed to the close link between the space and defense industries when it announced the deal.

Noting that global government spending on space defense accelerated to €65.83 billion last year, CSG estimates that the overall space economy will triple in size to €1.6 trillion over the next decade.

Developing capabilities in space is "a natural extension" of its activities, the company stated, noting plans for further development in the segment, including a "dedicated space team."

To power such missions, Czech defense companies must make sure they're in a position to tap into funds for defense and space under the next EU budget, which could rise as high as €130 billion, said Jires.

"If they fail to do so, and all this money is grabbed by German, French and Italian companies," he warned, "Czech manufacturers may miss the opportunity to truly scale-up."

November 6, 2026

Most people in Iran have little idea of the course of the US-led war and peace talks on the global stage. With few sources of information, the population must navigate conflicting rumors and fears of a nuclear attack.

"There is a constant sense of fear in the air," a 37-year-old mother in Tehran told DW. "Every time I hear a loud noise, I flinch. Even when a door slams, I jump — thinking that bombs are falling."

Now, unlike in the opening months of the war, her children are back at school.

"I don't work, but keeping the children at home out of fear is not a solution," she said. "They would go stir-crazy in our small apartment."

Iran's government takes aim at 'rumors'

Schools remain open across Iran despite the military standoff with the US and Israel. However, some parents whose children attend private schools have received messages from those schools explaining what to do in the event of a renewed war or other emergency.

Numerous parents have shared such messages on social media.

Irans Education Ministry has tried to reassure the public.

"People should not pay attention to rumors spread with the aim of sowing fear and forcing schools to close," Ali Farhadi, a ministry spokesperson, said in a recent media interview.

Farhadi said the ministry would decide whether the schools stay open or close, and would do so in coordination with the security authorities. Should the security outlook change, the situation will be reassessed accordingly, the official said.

'Pickaxe Mountain' at the center of nuclear attack fears

Parallel to Farhadi's appeal to disregard rumors aimed at raising fear, state media themselves are discussing scenarios of a possible nuclear attack.

On November 2, Iranian state television broadcast an advisory on protective measures in case of a nuclear strike. People were advised to remain in a shelter for at least 24 hours in the event of such an emergency.

Many in Iran fear that the United States is preparing to use nuclear weapons against the "Pickaxe Mountain" underground bunker about 220 kilometers (130 miles) south of Tehran. US President Donald Trump has hinted at attacking the location, which is close to Iran's Natanz nuclear facility, but made no explicit mention of using nuclear weapons.

Iran's government denies that any work related to its nuclear program is being carried out at the mountain bunker.

The fighting between the United States and Iran has mostly petered out in recent months as the Trump administration focused on the midterm election. But two days after the election, on November 5, the US news outlet Axios reported that the US military was making final preparations for a possible resumption of large-scale strikes against Iran.

Trump has 2 months before new Congress takes power

At the same time, there are also hopes that a Democrat-controlled Congress would force Trump to scale down his military ambitions.

"It is still difficult to make any concrete assessment of the implications of the US midterm election results for the war with Iran," Hamidreza Azizi, the International Crisis Group's consulting senior Iran analyst, wrote in response to questions from DW.

Iran's government sees the election results as a victory, Azizi wrote. The regime's resistance to the Trump administration has contributed to the Republican Party's loss in the US midterms, and some in Tehran are already seeking to frame the result as a sort of revenge for the US-Israeli assassination of senior Iranian leaders in the opening stages of the war.

Against this backdrop, Iran is likely to take an even harder line on its core demands.

Trump has at least two months before the new Congress takes office, Azizi wrote. He could decide to resume strikes on Iran in an attempt to offset a domestic political setback by targeting a foreign policy victory.

Reporters kept in the dark on peace talks

Qatari mediators are trying to persuade the Iranian and US governments to agree on a draft peace deal. The aim is to prevent another round of escalation and pave the way for the resumption of direct talks in the coming days.

But even well-connected journalists in Iran have little information on the substance of the talks, which are closed to the public.

In a post on X on October 31, the Iranian journalist Hadi Mohammadi wrote: "Domestic media outlets are completely in the dark about negotiations that directly affect people's everyday lives. They have to wait for reports from Axios, Al Arabiya, Al Jazeera and other international media outlets. In such an environment, developing our own narratives and doing journalism becomes pointless."

As the fog of war persists, many in Iran no longer have the energy to keep up with the media reporting. A 72-year-old retired woman from western Iran told DW she now deliberately avoids the news.

"I hardly have the strength to think about it anymore," she said. "I'm just glad that my three children have emigrated."

This article was originally published in German.

CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips.

The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

articles.body:
OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.

In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.

TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.

OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market, with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

articles.preview: Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity. The 12-year-old, North Andover, Massachusetts-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. articles.body:
Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity.

The 12-year-old, North Andover, Massachusetts-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. The plant will use a unique microwave-powered process to produce battery materials that don’t rely on Chinese suppliers.

The company previously received a $50 million grant from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, though that 2023 grant was canceled by the Trump administration in a chaotic sweep of Biden-era awards, forcing 6K to reapply.

The factory was originally slated to open in 2024, but the grant cancelation and uncertainties in the EV market forced the company to rejigger its plans.

6K’s manufacturing process uses microwaves to heat metals into a plasma and then deposit them onto a surface, reducing the number of steps required to make cathode material, a key battery component. The company says the process can work on a number of different battery types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

articles.title: Japan launches emergency cybersecurity package after wave of attacks
articles.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the package includes security countermeasures, strengthening of investigation systems and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage.
articles.preview: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the package includes security countermeasures, strengthening of investigation systems and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage. TOKYO: Japan launched a multimillion-dollar emergency policy package on Friday (Nov 6) to address a sudden wave of hacking incidents. The country's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has vowed to take action after dozens of businesses reported unauthorised access in recent weeks to their systems and potential leaks of client data.
articles.body:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the package includes security countermeasures, strengthening of investigation systems and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage.

TOKYO: Japan launched a multimillion-dollar emergency policy package on Friday (Nov 6) to address a sudden wave of hacking incidents.

The country's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has vowed to take action after dozens of businesses reported unauthorised access in recent weeks to their systems and potential leaks of client data.

Hacks and data breaches have ballooned worldwide, with AI's ability to find previously unknown ways to break into computer systems in the global spotlight.

"In light of the current situation involving increasingly serious cyberattacks, all ministers present today have put their heads together to formulate an 'emergency countermeasures package,'” Takaichi told her ministers on Friday.

The package would initially be funded by 10 billion yen (US$63 million) available in the government's budget but the overall cost would likely be higher, with the premier asking her finance minister to figure out how to free up funds for the entire plan.

The package includes security countermeasures partly through the use of AI, strengthening of investigation systems, and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage, she said.

Media reports have said the package includes the creation of a "cyber rescue team" made up of both government and private sector experts.

The government will set up a secretariat within the current fiscal year to coordinate the deployment of the rescue team when support needs are particularly acute, the Yomiuri Shimbun daily, Jiji Press and other reports said.

Takaichi did not mention the cyber rescue team but said that mobilisation was needed to "keep up with the speed of cyberattacks in the AI era.

"Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorised access and information leaks are occurring one after another, having a major impact on the lives of our citizens and on corporate activities," she said.

"Let us mobilise the full capabilities of the government to strengthen our nation’s overall capacity to respond," she added.

Chinese artificial intelligence cybersecurity tool Artex was used in several recent hacks of Japanese companies, an information security arm of Japanese IT firm GMO Internet Group Inc said last month.

GMO Internet Group itself is among those that have come under attack.

The hackers, identified by U.S. authorities as members of North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, have been seen transferring stolen assets through thousands of digital wallets and across multiple blockchains in an effort to obscure their origins.
articles.body:
Hackers behind the $6.3 billion theft from Binance Holdings are moving some of the stolen cryptocurrency through Chinese money-laundering networks, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.

The hackers, identified by U.S. authorities as members of North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, have been seen transferring stolen assets through thousands of digital wallets and across multiple blockchains in an effort to obscure their origins. North Korean hackers are said to have used Chinese money-laundering networks in previous thefts as well, and Chainalysis said that it’s tracked hundreds of thousands of dollars from the Binance theft — a fraction of the total stolen — flow into these networks.

The flows into money laundering networks, which include over-the-counter trading desks, suggest that hackers are pushing to take funds off of blockchain networks and cash them out, said Chainalysis.

articles.title: North Korea's army of world-class hackers is secret weapon that took down Binance
articles.summary: North Korea identifies top students from a young age, training a select few for cyber operations and rewarding them with perks such as spacious apartments and huge hard currency awards, defectors and analysts say.
articles.preview: North Korea identifies top students from a young age, training a select few for cyber operations and rewarding them with perks such as spacious apartments and huge hard currency awards, defectors and analysts say. SEOUL: North Korea rewards its top hackers, tasked with heists like the Binance crypto hack that netted US$6.3 billion, with perks such as a spacious apartment in the capital of Pyongyang and huge hard currency awards, despite gruelling hours of work.
articles.body:
North Korea identifies top students from a young age, training a select few for cyber operations and rewarding them with perks such as spacious apartments and huge hard currency awards, defectors and analysts say.

SEOUL: North Korea rewards its top hackers, tasked with heists like the Binance crypto hack that netted US$6.3 billion, with perks such as a spacious apartment in the capital of Pyongyang and huge hard currency awards, despite gruelling hours of work.

Leader Kim Jong Un has assembled an army of world-class hackers using such incentives in a programme more than a decade old that picks 200 of the smartest middle school students each year to study computer engineering, defectors and analysts say.

A fraction eventually become hackers in an investment that has paid off dramatically, as the group has evolved from the early days when it ran illegal gambling websites to pulling off the world's biggest cyber heist last month.

"They are actually one of Kim Jong Un's secret weapons," said Kim Heung-kwang, a North Korean defector who trained hackers of behalf of the state before fleeing to South Korea in 2004.

"There is no other country grooming hackers like this, systematically searching for the smartest children, solely to turn them into operatives," he added. "Whether they want to be a hacker or not does not matter."

The FBI and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the Binance hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. Blockchain investigation firms have attributed it to a North Korean group known as "TraderTraitor".

The denial is part of a pattern in which the North dismisses such blame over the years as fabricated political provocations.

SYSTEMIC SELECTION

North Korea set up a cyber unit in 1998 but elevated its status after Kim came to power and declared in 2013 that cyber warfare was, along with nuclear weapons and missiles, an "all-purpose sword" crucial to the country's strike capability.

Candidate selection begins in middle school as early as 11 or 12 years of age, with authorities picking about 150 to 200 children a year to study computer science, said Kim Heung-kwang, the former trainer, and two defectors who worked in IT.

At 17, the top performers are sent to North Korea's best universities and undergo further screening before a chosen few finally enter the military's cyber unit as hackers, they added.

They are trained in areas such as cryptocurrency protocols and reverse-engineering foreign hardware devices in addition to more conventional topics such as advanced mathematics and foreign languages, one of them said.

Those who do not become hackers are trained to turn out software or apps for Western firms via remote jobs.

"While South Korea's best students may pursue medicine or other prestigious careers, North Korea channels top talent into nuclear and cyber programs and essentially guarantees their future," said Lim Jongin, professor emeritus at the school of cybersecurity at Korea University.

Other privileges on tap for the hackers are travel abroad to allied countries, such as China, where they can more freely access the internet.

Successful exploits can earn as much as 30 per cent of the heist's profits in US dollars for the hackers' military unit, and they can even receive a flat in the capital where their parents can also stay, Kim said.

"There are accounts that successful cyber personnel are given apartments in Pyongyang," Lim said, adding that the flats could range to as much as 1,420 sq ft.

Such performers are also eligible for membership of the ruling party and high-status marriages into elite families, said one of the defectors.

But it is a small group. The North's cyberwarfare operations employ about 8,400 people, South Korea's National Intelligence Service estimated in 2024.

North Korean state media do not publicly celebrate such hackers' achievements, but they regularly highlight students who show talent for programming.

In 2015, North Korea opened the Mirae Scientists Street in the capital, in the construction of which Kim Jong Un had been closely involved, state media said.

Hackers' formal designation in the North was "scientist" or "researcher", said one of the defectors.

STATE ADVANTAGE

Other hacking groups associated with North Korea include the Lazarus Group, also known as APT38, which the US accused in 2022 of having stolen hundreds of millions of dollars worth of cryptocurrency from the Ronin blockchain network. The FBI has said TraderTraitor is affiliated to Lazarus.

State backing makes the North's hackers more dangerous and harder to repulse, as they face no consequences for hack after hack, enabling them to perfect their strategies, analysts said.

"In the world of cyber crime, often, if you make a mistake ... that is all law enforcement needs to get you," said Alec Zebrick, senior manager for Asia-Pacific global services at Chainalysis.

But North Korea's hackers "are doing this for the regime, so they're going to continue, even after successes", he added.

"Even after failures, they'll continue, because it's very hard for the international community to take action against them."

Other groups that have engaged with North Korea IT workers who earn funds for the Kim regime by landing remote technology jobs at Western companies describe them as highly organised, polite in their interactions and avid users of AI.

"There clearly was a structure you would see in military. Strict times, cleaning boots, very orderly," said YouTuber Deeveeaar, who has claimed to have hacked into cameras watching North Korean IT workers at their jobs.

"To say they 'use a lot of AI' is an understatement. AI is the very backbone of their operation," he said, citing use of paid ChatGPT accounts, Claude Code and Cursor, among many AI tools.

"They write code with it, alter their resumes and help make new ones. And even forge documents and identities."

Binance said the hackers used a bogus job interview and software hidden in an advertisement to compromise staffers' computers before using an internal AI tool to seize control of systems.

In 2025, a sanctions monitoring team drawn from 11 United Nations members said TraderTraitor had obtained both ChatGPT and DeepSeek accounts.

TOUGH WORKING CONDITIONS

Yet the lifestyle of a hacker or elite technology worker for North Korea is gruelling, particularly when given a mission or sent abroad, say former IT workers and human rights groups.

Living in cramped spaces, often working stretches longer than 10 hours a day, constant surveillance and strict targets are among the downsides, said former IT workers interviewed for a report last year by advocacy group PSCORE.

"There is always pressure to keep earning money," said the group's executive director, Nam Bada. "The stress is extreme, and because of the psychological strain people develop health problems they didn't have before."

IT workers must meet a monthly target in dollars, or face humiliation and other punishments, he said.

Still, the hackers' success is likely to embolden the North Korean leader as they get better and grow more ambitious, analysts say.

"We see more and more them leaning towards what we call 'big game hunting'," said Zebrick.

"So they're targeting some of these larger organisations, potentially have larger vaults of funds, that they could potentially get. These are harder targets," he added.

"However, as we can see with the Binance case, the payout certainly can make it worth their time."

articles.title: Cultura e creatività come volàno per l’economia: il bilancio di Eureka
articles.summary: Con un bilancio di oltre 260 incontri B2B, pianificati tramite agenda digitale fra le imprese espositrici e le aziende della tradizione, ha chiuso la terza edizione di Eureka, Fiera per...

articles.body:
A Pordenone chiusa la terza edizione della fiera promossa dalla Regione Autonoma Friuli Venezia Giulia - Realizzati oltre 260 incontri B2B

Con un bilancio di oltre 260 incontri B2B, pianificati tramite agenda digitale fra le imprese espositrici e le aziende della tradizione, ha chiuso la terza edizione di Eureka, Fiera per le Imprese Culturali e Creative promossa a Pordenone Fiere dalla Regione Autonoma Friuli Venezia Giulia.

È stata una opportunità di crescita e uno spazio concreto di business matching nel quale aziende ad alta innovazione e imprese del comparto manifatturiero e industriale hanno potuto dialogare e stringere nuove collaborazioni commerciali. Un circolo virtuoso che ha coinvolto anche brand nazionali, da Fincantieri (con Marine Interiors) a Crédit Agricole, intorno al tema sempre più importante dei Talenti Creativi in azienda.

«La due giorni - spiegano gli organizzatori - ha dimostrato nei fatti che inserire stabilmente designer, artisti ed esperti di storytelling all’interno delle divisioni strategiche e dei processi di Ricerca e Sviluppo permette alle aziende tradizionali di affrontare con maggiore competitività le complesse sfide dei mercati del nostro tempo». Eureka è l’unica vetrina nazionale dedicata alle Imprese Culturali e Creative: al centro dell’attenzione l’impatto macroeconomico della Creative Economy, settore capace di attivare un impatto complessivo di circa 310 miliardi di euro sull’intera economia nazionale, indotto incluso.

«La Regione Autonoma Friuli Venezia Giulia, che si distingue a livello nazionale per essere stata tra le prime amministrazioni a misurare scientificamente l’impatto economico della cultura sul Pil regionale, pari nel 2025 a oltre 2,1 miliardi di valore aggiunto, riafferma così la propria visione di “cultura di frontiera” – ha detto il vicepresidente della regione e assessore alla Cultura e allo Sport Mario Anzil - Un’infrastruttura strategica e un motore concreto di sviluppo in grado di valorizzare il capitale umano e alimentare la solidità della produzione industriale italiana sui mercati globali».

Una conferma «della capacità di Pordenone Fiere di essere non solo luogo espositivo, ma piattaforma di incontro tra competenze creative e sistema produttivo. Integrare creatività, innovazione e manifattura significa generare nuove opportunità di business e rafforzare la competitività delle imprese», ha spiegato il presidente di Pordenone Fiere Renato Pujatti.

articles.title: BOJ’s Ueda says unclear how long 2% inflation rate will remain
articles.summary: Gov. Kazuo Ueda indicated an awareness that the goal had been reached hasn't yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public.
articles.preview: Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda said that while his nation’s inflation rate has reached policymakers’ target, it’s unclear how long it will stay there, and indicated it hasn’t yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public. “Underlying inflation is 2% — our goal is to keep it there,” Ueda said in a question and answer session after delivering a speech at the International Monetary Fund in Washington on Friday. “I think we are in equilibrium,” he said.
articles.body:
Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda said that while his nation’s inflation rate has reached policymakers’ target, it’s unclear how long it will stay there, and indicated it hasn’t yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public.

“Underlying inflation is 2% — our goal is to keep it there,” Ueda said in a question and answer session after delivering a speech at the International Monetary Fund in Washington on Friday. “I think we are in equilibrium,” he said. “Whether we could stay in that equilibrium for a very long time to come, we still don’t know.”

The remarks come a week after the BOJ marked a milestone by declaring that underlying inflation had reached the bank’s 2% target for the first time since the goal was introduced in 2013. Ueda didn’t offer any specific guidance on the central bank’s appetite to raise interest rates further, in an exchange with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.

articles.body:
Hakeem Jeffries, the leader of House Democrats, promises to “stop the stupid Trump tariffs jacking up prices on Americans.” Ron Wyden, incoming Senate Finance Committee chairman, says he’ll reassert congressional authority over trade policy. Even Senator Ted Cruz, the Texas Republican, lamented that “tariffs have made everything too expensive.”

But curbing President Donald Trump’s tariff powers won’t be easy or quick, and there’s a risk any efforts to do so in the incoming Democratic-led Congress will spur infighting in both parties.

While the president tempered his policies ahead of Tuesday’s election, he has several potential trade barriers in the pipeline. Trump could announce a new set of duties linked to excess industrial capacity that would hit imports from more than a dozen economies — even before Democrats take control in January.

Presentata la nuova edizione davanti a 600 studenti. Percorso con 50 parole chiave. Lagarde (Bce): «Grazie all’Osservatorio per il suo lavoro sull’alfabetizzazione economico-finanziaria»

Capire l’economia e la finanza per scegliere il futuro. Young Factor Europe porta l’educazione economico-finanziaria nelle scuole superiori di sei Paesi, con una piattaforma gratuita e un percorso costruito su 50 parole chiave. Andrea Ceccherini, fondatore e presidente di Osservatorio for Independent Thinking, ha presentato la nuova edizione a Milano davanti alla presidente Bce Christine Lagarde e a 600 studenti.

Ceccherini: «Esercizio per partecipare alla vita democratica»

La posta in gioco supera la gestione dei risparmi: «Studiare la finanza e l’economia – spiega Ceccherini – è oggi un esercizio per partecipare a pieno titolo alla democrazia». Quello dell’alfabetizzazione economico-finanziaria,ha commentato la governatrice della Bce, è «un tema che mi sta particolarmente a cuore e che considero una componente essenziale della libertà: in particolare per le donne, conoscere gli strumenti finanziari e disporre delle competenze necessarie per gestire le proprie risorse significa poter compiere scelte autonome e decidere del proprio futuro». Da qui il «ringraziamento» all’Osservatorio per l’alto valore civile dell’iniziativa e «per il lavoro che sta facendo».

Le Cinquanta parole

termini Il progetto è in fase pilota avanzata in Italia, Germania e Spagna e avviata in Francia, Paesi Bassi e Portogallo. Nel nostro Paese il progetto è sostenuto da Intesa Sanpaolo e UniCredit ai quali si aggiungerà anche Crédit Agricole Italia.

Il fulcro sono 50 parole, spiegate e illustrate, che si affrontano in cinque anni: test per misurare le conoscenze, videolezioni, attualità, masterclass dei governatori delle banche centrali e attività pratiche. A disposizione di docenti e studenti il giornalismo di Financial Times, The Economist, Wall Street Journal e Sole 24 Ore, attraverso la piattaforma Doubt and Debate.

Lagarde: «Questioni finanziarie ancora poco capite»

Quanto sia necessario questo alfabeto lo indica la stessa Lagarde parlando davanti agli studenti a Milano: in Europa, osserva, «il 50% dei cittadini ha una comprensione molto limitata delle questioni finanziarie. C’è chi fatica a distinguere un tasso fisso da uno variabile». Lacune che si riflettono sulla capacità di valutare un’offerta, gestire le proprie risorse e decidere con consapevolezza.
